corrective_actions: Increase sample concentration to 0.5–5 mg/mL for proteins, 0.01–1 mg/mL for nanoparticles
Verify correct measurement position is selected for the cell type (cuvette vs. capillary vs. back scatter)
Set correct material refractive index in software (1.45 for proteins, 1.59 for polystyrene, 1.5 for liposomes)
Check laser shutter is open and laser is operating normally
escalation_conditions: Count rate is zero even with a known scattering standard — laser or detector failure, contact Malvern Panalytical service

symptom: Absolute molecular weight from SEC-MALS differs significantly from expected value; inconsistent with SDS-PAGE or mass spec data
likely_causes: Incorrect dn/dc value entered — dn/dc error propagates directly to MW with 1:1 sensitivity
Inter-detector delay volumes miscalibrated — LS, RI, and UV peak maxima not aligned
Protein has unusual dn/dc due to glycosylation, conjugation, or post-translational modifications
RI baseline drift affecting concentration accuracy
Column overloading causing non-ideal separation and apparent mass shift
diagnostics: Run BSA monomer standard (66.4 kDa) — proteins in PBS have dn/dc = 0.185 mL/g
Verify inter-detector delay volumes by overlaying LS, RI, and UV peak maxima in ASTRA
Check RI baseline stability — drift > 0.5 × 10⁻⁶ RIU/min affects accuracy
Reduce injection concentration by 5× and compare MW result
corrective_actions: Re-determine dn/dc by offline batch measurement or use published value for the molecule class
Recalibrate inter-detector delay volumes using monodisperse BSA standard in ASTRA
Equilibrate RI detector for 1–2 h before analysis
Reduce injection concentration to 1–2 mg/mL
For glycoproteins or conjugates, use conjugate analysis module in ASTRA
escalation_conditions: MW error persists after dn/dc correction and delay volume recalibration — contact Wyatt Technology support for detector normalization check

symptom: MALS signal shows high noise, spikes, or irreproducible scattering; baseline noisy between peaks
likely_causes: Particulates or aggregates in mobile phase scattering randomly into detectors
Air bubbles in flow path — micro-bubbles scatter light strongly
Flow cell contaminated with protein or excipient film
Temperature instability in DAWN detector housing
Mobile phase not filtered through 0.1 µm inline filter
diagnostics: Run mobile phase blank — if noise is present with blank, it is flow-path-related
Inspect high-angle detectors (90°, 120°) — most sensitive to particles
Degas mobile phase and check for bubbles at pump head
Check DAWN temperature log — instability > 0.1 °C correlates with LS noise
corrective_actions: Filter all mobile phases through 0.1 µm Durapore filter
Degas mobile phase under vacuum for 15 min before use
Clean DAWN flow cell with 0.1 µm filtered 1 M NaOH then mobile phase flush
Filter sample through 0.2 µm PVDF immediately before injection
Allow DAWN to temperature-equilibrate for 1+ hour before measurement
escalation_conditions: Noise persists after mobile phase filtration and flow cell cleaning — contact Wyatt Technology for flow cell replacement or laser check

symptom: RI detector baseline drifts during run; pre-peak and post-peak baselines are not flat
likely_causes: RI detector not fully equilibrated — requires 30–60 min at stable temperature
Ambient temperature fluctuations
Mobile phase composition changing due to differential evaporation
Pump flow rate pulsing causing RI oscillation
Reference cell contaminated or not filled with fresh mobile phase
diagnostics: Monitor baseline for 30+ min before injection — drift should be < 1 × 10⁻⁷ RIU/min; drift > 5 × 10⁻⁷ RIU/min will compromise molecular weight accuracy significantly
Check column oven and detector temperature stability using system monitoring: RI signal is extremely sensitive to temperature — 0.01 °C change can produce measurable baseline shift
Compare drift with and without pump running: if drift disappears when pump stops, the issue is flow-related (pump pulsation, mobile phase composition change); if drift persists, it is thermal
Check if drift correlates with laboratory HVAC cycling: plot RI baseline alongside room temperature recorded by datalogger — periodic drift matching HVAC cycle confirms environmental cause

Measure RI baseline at two different wavelengths if multi-wavelength RI is available — wavelength-dependent drift indicates solvent composition change; wavelength-independent drift indicates temperature fluctuation
Verify mobile phase reservoir is sealed to prevent evaporation: differential evaporation of organic component changes refractive index of mobile phase over time, causing progressive baseline drift
Check for air dissolving into mobile phase during the run: as mobile phase warms from room temperature to column oven temperature, dissolved gas forms microbubbles that scatter light in the RI cell
Inspect RI cell windows for scratches or deposits by running water baseline and comparing to specification: contaminated windows cause permanent baseline offset and increased noise
corrective_actions: Allow RI detector to equilibrate for minimum 60 min — connect to mobile phase flow and run at analysis flow rate; some RI detectors (Optilab, OMNISEC) require 90+ min for sub-1e-7 drift
Position RI detector away from air vents, drafts, windows, and laboratory doors — use a cardboard or foam enclosure around the detector to minimize ambient temperature fluctuation
Use HPLC-grade solvent filtered through 0.1 µm (not 0.2 µm) for SEC-MALS: larger particles scatter light and create both LS noise and RI artifacts
Flush reference cell with fresh mobile phase: disconnect reference cell, flush with 20 mL of current mobile phase, then reconnect — stale mobile phase in reference cell causes progressive drift
Add backpressure regulator (50–75 psi) after the RI detector to keep dissolved gases in solution through the flow cell — prevents micro-bubble formation that causes RI spikes
Seal mobile phase reservoirs with minimal headspace and use helium sparging or online degassing to prevent dissolved oxygen and CO2 from changing solvent refractive index during long runs
Clean RI cell windows per manufacturer procedure: flush with 1 M NaOH (30 min), then water (30 min), then mobile phase (30 min) — never use abrasive cleaning on optical-grade windows
escalation_conditions: Baseline drift > 5 × 10⁻⁷ RIU/min after 2+ hours equilibration — contact Malvern Panalytical service

symptom: Large high-MW peak at void volume; MALS reports extremely high apparent MW for early-eluting peak
likely_causes: Protein or biopolymer aggregating in formulation buffer
Sample concentration too high causing concentration-dependent aggregation
Aggregates not removed prior to injection
Multiple freeze-thaw cycles causing aggregation
Sample exposed to elevated temperature during preparation
diagnostics: Compare UV A280 and LS signals for early peak: very high LS/UV ratio (> 10× that of monomer peak) indicates large aggregates — aggregates scatter light much more intensely per unit mass than monomers
Calculate apparent Rg (radius of gyration) for the void volume peak using ASTRA or OMNISEC software — aggregates typically show Rg > 50 nm vs. monomer Rg of 2–5 nm for typical antibodies
Filter sample through 0.2 µm PVDF syringe filter and compare chromatograms: if void peak disappears after filtration, the aggregates are > 200 nm and removable
Quantify aggregate content as % of total UV peak area: regulatory threshold for biopharmaceuticals is typically < 2% high molecular weight species (HMWS) for clinical material

Acquire UV spectrum (if DAD available) across the void volume peak: protein aggregates show characteristic 280 nm absorption proportional to aromatic amino acid content; non-protein aggregates show different spectral profile
Run DLS on unfiltered sample to independently assess particle size distribution: DLS will show the aggregate population that SEC-MALS detects, confirming the size range
Check sample storage conditions: review temperature, time since thaw, container material, and number of previous freeze-thaw cycles — each factor accelerates aggregation

Inject at multiple concentrations (0.5, 1, 2, 5 mg/mL) to distinguish concentration-dependent reversible association from irreversible aggregation — reversible association decreases at lower concentration
corrective_actions: Filter sample through 0.2 µm PVDF immediately before injection — use low-protein-binding membrane (Millex-GV or Pall Acrodisc PVDF) to minimize protein loss during filtration
Reduce sample concentration to 1–2 mg/mL to minimize concentration-dependent self-association and column overloading effects
Optimize formulation buffer: adjust pH (±0.5 unit), increase ionic strength (150 mM NaCl), or add stabilizers (0.01% polysorbate 80, 5% sucrose) to reduce aggregation propensity
Minimize freeze-thaw cycles: aliquot sample into single-use volumes at −80 °C; thaw slowly at 4 °C rather than at room temperature to reduce cold denaturation risk
If aggregation is time-dependent: prepare fresh sample immediately before injection and compare to stored sample — this establishes whether aggregation is pre-existing or forms during storage
For critical biopharmaceutical samples: use multiple orthogonal methods (SEC-MALS, AUC, FFF-MALS) to fully characterize the aggregate profile for regulatory submissions
Implement routine SEC-MALS stability monitoring: track % HMWS over time at 2–8 °C, 25 °C, and 40 °C accelerated conditions to predict product shelf life
escalation_conditions: Aggregate content > 5% in biopharmaceutical product — investigate formulation and process conditions

symptom: LS, RI, and UV detectors report different elution times for the same peak apex; MW shows systematic slope across molar mass profile
likely_causes: Inter-detector delay volumes changed after column replacement or system reconfiguration
Flow cell replaced without re-normalization
Tubing lengths changed from last calibration
Software delay volume settings not updated after hardware modification
diagnostics: Overlay LS (90°), RI, and UV (280 nm) signals for BSA monomer peak: all three detector peaks should align within 0.001 min (< 1 µL volume difference at 0.5 mL/min) — offset indicates incorrect delay volume in software

Check molar mass profile across BSA monomer peak: ideal result is flat line at 66.4 kDa; upward slope from left to right indicates LS detector sees peak before RI (LS delay volume too small); downward slope is the reverse
Use Normalize Detectors wizard in ASTRA: run BSA monomer standard, and ASTRA automatically calculates normalization coefficients and delay volumes for each detector in the array
Inject narrow polystyrene standard (e.g., 30 kDa PS, PDI < 1.05) as independent verification: narrowly dispersed standards are more sensitive to delay volume errors than BSA
Check all inter-detector tubing lengths with a ruler: calculate expected delay volume from tubing ID and length — V = π × (ID/2)² × length — compare to software setting
Run the same BSA standard at two different flow rates (0.3 and 0.7 mL/min): if delay volumes are correctly set in volume units, MW results should be identical at both flow rates
Verify UV detector wavelength is set correctly: 280 nm for protein at standard concentration; if UV and RI peaks are offset, check whether UV path length matches the RI path through the system
After column replacement: always re-run delay volume calibration because new column void volume differs from previous column, shifting all peak elution times relative to detector positions
corrective_actions: Run delay volume calibration in ASTRA using BSA monomer (2 mg/mL in PBS, 100 µL injection): ASTRA calculates inter-detector delay volumes automatically from the BSA peak alignment
Re-normalize DAWN detectors using toluene or BSA following the ASTRA normalization procedure: each detector angle is normalized to the 90° detector signal to correct for angle-dependent scattering
Record flow path configuration in instrument logbook: document tubing lengths, IDs, and detector order — update ASTRA method file whenever any plumbing change is made
After any hardware change (column, tubing, detector cell), always recalibrate delay volumes before running samples — incorrect delay volumes propagate directly into MW errors
Verify calibration by measuring BSA dimer (133 kDa) and monomer (66.4 kDa) peaks: both should report correct MW within ±5% to confirm delay volumes are accurate across the elution profile
Save calibrated method as a template and use for all subsequent experiments — maintain separate templates for different column/flow rate combinations
escalation_conditions: MW profile shows systematic slope despite recalibration — contact Wyatt Technology for detector check

symptom: TEM images lack sharpness, show low contrast, or cannot resolve expected structural details
likely_causes: Objective lens astigmatism — most common cause of blurry TEM images
Sample too thick — insufficient electron transmission for BF imaging
Insufficient or excessive staining (negative stain TEM)
Contaminated objective aperture causing aberrations
Incorrect focus — slight underfocus required for phase contrast
diagnostics: Check power spectrum (FFT) of amorphous region — circular Thon rings confirm good astigmatism
Measure sample thickness — thick areas appear dark; reduce for better transmission
Inspect objective aperture for contamination
Verify defocus value — optimal BF TEM uses −200 to −2000 nm underfocus
corrective_actions: Correct objective astigmatism using stigmator controls in TEM software
Prepare thinner specimens — dilute sample or use ion milling
Optimize negative stain concentration (2% uranyl acetate or 1% uranyl formate)
Plasma-clean or replace objective aperture
Adjust defocus to optimal underfocus
escalation_conditions: Astigmatism cannot be corrected — contact Thermo Fisher service for objective lens alignment

symptom: Sample visibly changes under the electron beam; holes appear; nanoparticles sinter; crystalline regions become amorphous
likely_causes: Beam current too high for radiation-sensitive material
Accelerating voltage too high — higher kV increases radiolytic damage for organics
Long pre-exposure before image capture
Cryo samples sublimating due to warm anti-contaminator
diagnostics: Observe sample shrinkage rate by acquiring sequential images at 10-second intervals: fast shrinkage (visible within 30 s) indicates severe beam damage; slow shrinkage may be tolerable for quick imaging
Check spot size and condenser settings — larger spot = lower current density = less damage per unit area; compare damage rate at spot sizes 3, 5, and 7
For cryo-TEM: monitor ice quality for devitrification — crystalline ice produces sharp diffraction spots that are absent in vitreous ice; devitrified ice indicates sample warmed above −140 °C
Acquire electron diffraction pattern before and after imaging: loss of crystalline diffraction spots confirms radiation-induced amorphization of beam-sensitive crystalline materials
Calculate electron dose: dose (e⁻/Å²) = beam current × exposure time / illuminated area — most biological samples tolerate < 20 e⁻/Å² total dose; pharmaceutical crystals vary widely
Check for mass loss by monitoring zero-loss peak in EELS (if available) — mass loss manifests as spectral changes in the low-loss region and indicates radiolytic decomposition
Compare images at same magnification with and without pre-irradiation: if first-exposure image shows intact structure but subsequent images show damage, low-dose imaging is essential
Monitor for carbon contamination buildup: dark halo around irradiated area indicates hydrocarbon polymerization under beam — plasma clean grid before loading to reduce contamination
corrective_actions: Reduce accelerating voltage to 80 kV or lower for organic/biological materials — lower voltage reduces knock-on damage but increases radiolytic damage; find optimal voltage for your sample type
Use low-dose imaging mode: align and focus on adjacent area (> 3 µm away), then expose target area only during final image acquisition — minimizes cumulative radiation dose
Reduce beam current using larger spot size or smaller condenser aperture — trade-off is longer exposure time, but total dose per image is reduced
For cryo-TEM: maintain specimen below −170 °C throughout by keeping anti-contaminator filled with LN2 and minimizing specimen holder transfer time from LN2 to column
Use direct electron detector (DED) cameras (e.g., Gatan K3, Thermo Fisher Falcon 4) which provide higher DQE, allowing useful images at lower electron dose
Plasma clean TEM grids before sample application: 30 s H2/O2 plasma removes hydrocarbon contamination that polymerizes under beam, reducing contamination-related artifacts
For dose-sensitive crystallography: collect diffraction data using automated serial acquisition (MicroED) to distribute dose across many crystals rather than destroying a single crystal
escalation_conditions: Sample destroyed before usable image — consider cryo-TEM to preserve native structure

symptom: TEM column vacuum insufficient for beam activation; instrument prevents operation due to poor vacuum
likely_causes: Sample or grid outgassing — solvent residues or staining reagent not fully dried
Gun valve or airlock O-ring damaged
Ion pump degraded — pump current too low
Anti-contaminator not at LN2 temperature
Gun tip contaminated and degassing
diagnostics: Monitor vacuum gauges for each column section: gun (< 1e-8 Torr), column (< 1e-7 Torr), projection (< 1e-6 Torr) — identify which section is elevated to narrow the leak location
Fill anti-contaminator with LN2 and monitor vacuum improvement over 10 min — if vacuum improves significantly, outgassing species are being cryo-trapped, confirming contamination source
Check ion pump current reading in TEM software — below specification indicates pump failure; gradual increase over weeks indicates pump aging
Perform leak check: close all valves, monitor pressure rise rate — a fast rise (> 1e-7 Torr/min) indicates a real leak; slow rise indicates outgassing from contaminated components
Check specimen airlock sequence: verify that pre-pump and high-vacuum interlocks complete successfully — failed interlock prevents specimen insertion and protects the column from pressure burst
Inspect O-rings on specimen holder, airlock door, and column ports for damage, debris, or loss of elasticity — a single damaged O-ring can prevent achieving base vacuum
Monitor roughing pump status: exhaust should be clear and odorless; oil smoke or unusual noise indicates pump service is overdue — degraded roughing pump extends pump-down time significantly
Check for recent sample types that may have introduced contamination: biological stains (uranyl acetate, OsO4), volatile solvents, or uncured epoxy can outgas for days after a single specimen
corrective_actions: Dry grids in desiccator for 30+ min before loading — for negative stain grids, ensure stain is fully dried; residual water from uranyl acetate extends pump-down time by 10–20 min
Fill anti-contaminator with fresh LN2 before each session — verify LN2 level is adequate for the full session duration (typically 4–6 hour hold time per fill)
Replace airlock O-rings on scheduled maintenance: every 12 months or whenever damaged — use manufacturer-specified Viton O-rings; clean O-ring grooves with IPA before installing new rings
Contact Thermo Fisher service for ion pump regeneration (bakeout at 300 °C under turbo pump vacuum) or replacement if current remains low after regeneration
Perform column bakeout if outgassing contamination is suspected: heat column to 120–150 °C under turbo pump vacuum for 12–24 hours — this removes adsorbed contaminants from pole pieces and apertures
Clean specimen holder: wipe with ethanol-dampened lint-free tissue, dry with nitrogen, and check O-ring condition before each loading — contaminated holders are a frequent vacuum degradation source
Maintain roughing pump oil level and change oil every 6–12 months per manufacturer schedule — degraded oil reduces pump ultimate vacuum and extends column pump-down time
escalation_conditions: Column vacuum cannot be achieved with dry specimen — column bakeout required; contact Thermo Fisher service

symptom: Specimen drifts during image acquisition; serial images show translational shift; long-exposure images appear directionally blurred
likely_causes: Thermal drift — grid warming from beam irradiation
Mechanical vibration from building or nearby equipment
Grid not fully seated in specimen holder
Cryo holder thermal drift due to fluctuating LN2 supply
diagnostics: Measure drift rate in nm/s using dedicated drift measurement tool in TEM software — acceptable drift for high-resolution imaging is < 0.5 nm/s; for cryo-EM single particle analysis, drift should be < 1 nm/s during movie acquisition

Pre-irradiate area at lower magnification for 30–60 s before high-mag imaging — beam-induced local heating causes most drift in the first 30 s; drift rate decreases exponentially as thermal equilibrium is reached

Check for vibration sources in room: HVAC systems, rotating equipment (centrifuges, compressors), and foot traffic all couple to the TEM through floor vibrations — measure with accelerometer if available

Acquire two sequential images at the same magnification and cross-correlate to calculate drift vector: consistent direction indicates thermal gradient or holder issue; random direction suggests vibration
Monitor cryo-holder temperature stability: temperature fluctuation > 1 °C causes thermal expansion drift in the specimen rod — verify LN2 level and dewar thermal contact
Check that specimen holder is fully inserted and locked: partially seated holders have mechanical play that manifests as drift, especially when stage is tilted
Assess whether drift is beam-induced by blanking beam for 60 s, then imaging: if drift decreases after blanking, it is thermally driven by beam heating
Verify anti-vibration table (if installed) is properly leveled and pressurized: air-table systems lose effectiveness if pneumatic pressure drops or if loads are unbalanced
corrective_actions: Allow 15–30 min thermal equilibration after loading specimen before high-magnification imaging — longer equilibration for cryo-holders that require temperature stabilization after LN2 transfer
Pre-irradiate region of interest at low magnification (2000–5000×) for 30–60 s to thermally stabilize the local area before switching to high magnification

Use rapid acquisition: short exposure times (< 1 s) or movie mode with dose fractionation and post-acquisition drift correction — drift correction algorithms in software (e.g., MotionCor2) compensate for residual drift
Clean specimen holder and replace O-ring per maintenance schedule — contaminated or worn O-rings cause outgassing that creates thermal gradients and drives drift

Isolate TEM from building vibrations: use active damping table, schedule high-resolution sessions during low-traffic hours (evenings/weekends), and request that nearby equipment be turned off during critical sessions
For cryo-EM: ensure LN2 dewar is filled to appropriate level and thermal braid contact with holder is secure — intermittent thermal contact causes periodic temperature fluctuations and drift
escalation_conditions: Drift rate > 2 nm/s after 30 min equilibration — specimen holder service required

symptom: TEM images show directional blurring; FFT power spectrum shows elliptical Thon rings
likely_causes: Contaminated or damaged objective aperture — most common cause
Contaminated objective lens pole piece
Incorrect stigmator settings after column vent
Sample holder introducing magnetic field near objective lens
diagnostics: Acquire FFT (Fast Fourier Transform) of amorphous region at Scherzer defocus — circular Thon rings confirm correct astigmatism; elliptical rings with > 5% ellipticity confirm significant astigmatism requiring correction
Remove objective aperture and recheck FFT — if astigmatism disappears with aperture removed, the aperture is contaminated and is the source; if astigmatism persists, it is in the lens system
Compare current stigmator X/Y values to reference values recorded after last successful alignment — large deviation (> 10% of full range) suggests contamination-driven astigmatism

Image a standard test specimen (crossed lines grating or gold particles on amorphous carbon) and evaluate directional resolution difference — astigmatism makes features sharp in one direction and blurred 90° away
Check whether astigmatism is focus-dependent: acquire FFT at multiple defocus values — astigmatism from aperture contamination is approximately constant, while lens astigmatism may vary with current

Inspect condenser astigmatism separately: expand beam to full screen and check for elliptical illumination — condenser astigmatism is independent of objective astigmatism and has its own stigmator controls
Test with a different objective aperture from the aperture strip — if a clean aperture resolves the issue, the original aperture needs cleaning or replacement
For cryo-EM: check that specimen is not tilted on the grid — tilted ice surfaces create apparent astigmatism from defocus gradient across the field of view
corrective_actions: Plasma-clean objective aperture for 60 s using H2/O2 or Ar plasma cleaner — removes hydrocarbon contamination that is the most common cause of aperture-induced astigmatism
Re-correct astigmatism with stigmators on amorphous carbon film: adjust X and Y stigmators iteratively while monitoring FFT until Thon rings are circular — start at 100k× magnification
Record and save corrected stigmator values in TEM software after successful correction — these values serve as baseline for future sessions and can detect gradual contamination trends
Contact Thermo Fisher service if pole piece contamination is suspected — pole piece cleaning requires partial column disassembly and is not a user-serviceable operation
Replace the objective aperture if plasma cleaning does not restore circular Thon rings — apertures degrade over time from beam damage and sputtering
For persistent astigmatism after all corrections: perform full gun-to-camera alignment including pivot points, beam tilt, and rotation center — consult TEM manufacturer alignment guide
escalation_conditions: Astigmatism cannot be corrected after aperture replacement — objective lens pole piece cleaning required

symptom: Raman spectrum dominated by a broad fluorescence background that overwhelms Raman peaks
likely_causes: Sample intrinsically fluorescent — aromatic rings, porphyrins, dyes, pharmaceutical impurities
Surface contamination with fluorescent species (oils, fingerprints)
Short excitation wavelength (532 nm) exciting more fluorescence than 785 nm or 1064 nm
Photodegradation products are fluorescent
diagnostics: Identify fluorescence — Raman peaks are fixed in cm⁻¹; fluorescence shifts with excitation wavelength in nm
Try photobleaching — illuminate sample 5–30 min at reduced power
Switch to longer excitation wavelength (785 nm or 1064 nm)
Measure clean substrate — if it also fluoresces, contamination is the source
corrective_actions: Switch to 785 nm or 1064 nm excitation
Pre-bleach sample with low laser power for 10–30 min
Clean sample surface with appropriate solvent
Apply polynomial or spline background subtraction in software
Consider FTIR-ATR as alternative for strongly fluorescent samples
escalation_conditions: Fluorescence saturates detector even with 1064 nm excitation — sample incompatible with Raman; use FTIR

symptom: Sharp, extremely narrow spikes at random wavenumber positions; spikes are much taller than Raman peaks and appear inconsistently
likely_causes: High-energy cosmic ray or muon striking the CCD detector — unavoidable
Electrical noise spike on CCD read-out (usually reproducible)
Radioactive emission from sample (very rare)
diagnostics: Acquire two consecutive spectra of same spot — cosmic rays appear in only one spectrum
Enable cosmic ray removal in WiRE or LabSpec software
Check if spike position is consistent — if fixed, it is not a cosmic ray
corrective_actions: Enable automatic cosmic ray removal in Raman software (WiRE, LabSpec, OMNIC)
Use multiple short accumulations averaged — reduces cosmic ray probability
Manually delete spike in post-processing if filter missed it
escalation_conditions: Spikes appear at same position every acquisition — CCD hot pixel; contact Renishaw service

symptom: Sample physically changes under the laser; color changes, holes appear, or new broad bands indicate thermal decomposition
likely_causes: Laser power too high for absorbing sample
Long acquisition time at high power on sensitive pharmaceutical sample
Focused beam on small particle — high power density even at moderate overall power
Sample on insulating substrate with poor heat dissipation
diagnostics: Inspect sample under microscope after measurement — color change or hole confirms burning
Acquire successive spectra — if spectrum changes over time, thermal degradation occurring
Reduce power to 1–10% and repeat
Monitor for D/G bands at ~1350/1580 cm⁻¹ indicating carbonization
corrective_actions: Reduce laser power using neutral density filters
Increase scan speed or reduce exposure time
Defocus slightly from sample surface to reduce power density
Use longer excitation wavelength with lower photon energy
Disperse sample in KBr or on inert substrate for better heat dissipation
escalation_conditions: Sample burns at any laser power — consider ATR-FTIR or solid-state NMR as alternatives

symptom: Raman peaks appear at incorrect wavenumber positions; peak positions drift between sessions
likely_causes: Laser wavelength drift due to temperature change
Grating position drift in spectrograph
Calibration standard not measured before session
CCD temperature not stabilized
diagnostics: Measure silicon wafer (520.7 ± 0.5 cm⁻¹) and compare to expected value: shift > 0.5 cm⁻¹ requires recalibration; note both the absolute position and any asymmetry in the silicon peak shape

Check if wavenumber shift is consistent across the spectral range or wavelength-dependent: measure silicon (520.7 cm⁻¹), polystyrene (1001.4 cm⁻¹), and naphthalene (1382 cm⁻¹) — consistent offset indicates laser drift; variable offset indicates grating or detector calibration error
Verify laser warm-up time: minimum 30 min for diode-pumped solid-state lasers, 60 min for gas lasers (He-Ne) — measure silicon peak position at 5, 15, 30, and 60 min to track laser stabilization
Check CCD temperature: verify thermoelectric cooler is at setpoint (typically −70 °C for CCD) — elevated CCD temperature causes thermal expansion of the detector, shifting apparent peak positions
Inspect grating for dust or damage: switch between available gratings (600, 1200, 1800 gr/mm) and check if calibration error changes — grating-specific error indicates grating issue rather than laser
Verify spectrometer entrance slit width is at the calibrated value: changing slit width shifts the apparent peak centroid for asymmetric peaks, causing apparent calibration drift
Check room temperature stability: spectrometer components expand/contract with temperature, shifting calibration — record room temperature at time of calibration and during measurements
Run neon lamp emission lines to verify detector pixel-to-wavelength mapping: neon provides reference lines across the visible and near-IR range for comprehensive wavelength verification
corrective_actions: Warm up laser for minimum 30 min before calibration — do not acquire final calibration until silicon peak position is stable within ±0.1 cm⁻¹ over 3 consecutive measurements
Re-calibrate with silicon wafer (520.7 ± 0.5 cm⁻¹) at start of each session — use a freshly cleaved or polished silicon wafer; contaminated silicon shows shifted or broadened peak
Use neon lamp for full spectral range calibration: neon emission lines at 585.2, 614.3, 640.2, 703.2 nm provide reference points spanning the typical Raman spectral range
Update calibration file in software after each re-calibration — WiRE, LabSpec, and OMNIC all support automated silicon or neon calibration routines
If calibration drift occurs within a session (intra-session drift): enable auto-calibration feature if available, or bracket measurements with silicon reference checks every 2 hours

For precise polymorph identification (e.g., pharmaceutical crystal forms): verify calibration accuracy to < 0.5 cm⁻¹ by measuring a secondary standard (4-acetamidophenol polymorphs or cyclohexane) in addition to silicon
escalation_conditions: Wavenumber error > 2 cm⁻¹ after silicon calibration — contact Renishaw service for grating drive check

symptom: Raman signal too weak to observe meaningful peaks; SNR insufficient for quantitative analysis
likely_causes: Sample has intrinsically weak Raman cross-section
Laser power too low or ND filter engaged
Incorrect focus — objective not at sample surface
Sample too dilute for direct measurement
Wrong objective — insufficient numerical aperture
diagnostics: Check laser power at sample position using calibrated power meter: actual power at sample should match the software setting — losses of > 50% indicate beam path obstruction, dirty optics, or misaligned fiber coupling
Verify focus by observing reflected laser spot through the microscope video camera: the spot should be sharp and centered on the sample — defocused spot loses > 90% of collection efficiency

Increase accumulation (number of co-added scans) and check if SNR improves as √N: if SNR improves predictably, the issue is simply weak Raman scattering; if SNR does not improve, there is systematic noise (fluorescence, detector dark current)

Check that the correct confocal pinhole or slit width is set: too narrow reduces signal; too wide reduces spatial resolution and increases background — for bulk measurement, open confocal aperture to maximum

Verify notch or edge filter is appropriate for the excitation wavelength: a 785 nm filter will block all signal if used with a 532 nm laser — mismatch causes complete signal loss below the filter cutoff
Test with a strong Raman scatterer (silicon at 520.7 cm⁻¹, polystyrene at 1001 cm⁻¹): if strong signal from reference but not from sample, the issue is sample-specific, not instrumental

Check spectrometer grating selection: higher groove density gratings (1800 gr/mm) provide better spectral resolution but lower throughput; switch to 600 gr/mm for maximum signal at the expense of resolution
Inspect objective lens for cleanliness: fingerprints, sample residue, or immersion oil on the objective front element reduce both excitation delivery and signal collection efficiency
corrective_actions: Increase laser power (while staying below sample damage threshold) and increase acquisition time — doubling power doubles signal; doubling time improves SNR by √2
Use high-NA objective for maximum collection efficiency: 50× (0.75 NA) or 100× (0.9 NA) for solids; water-immersion objective for biological samples — higher NA collects more scattered light
Concentrate sample or use pellet press for solid pharmaceuticals: pressing powder into a dense pellet increases Raman signal per unit volume and reduces scatter from particle boundaries
Switch to resonance Raman wavelength if sample contains chromophore: excitation near absorption maximum enhances Raman signal by 10²–10⁶× — but also increases fluorescence risk

Remove neutral density filters from beam path if inadvertently engaged: check software power setting and physical filter wheel position — some systems default to reduced power after laser safety interlock reset
Clean objective lens with lens tissue and optical-grade ethanol: wipe in circular motion from center outward; verify clean by examining reflected laser spot through camera
For aqueous solutions: use immersion or water-dipping objective to eliminate air/glass/water interface reflections that reduce both excitation and collection efficiency
escalation_conditions: No signal even at maximum power with pure reference material — detector or laser failure; contact vendor service

symptom: MAS rotor fails to reach or maintain target spinning speed; speed below setpoint or unstable
likely_causes: Rotor not balanced correctly — asymmetric sample loading
Bearing gas pressure too low or contaminated
Drive gas flow insufficient for target spinning frequency
Rotor chipped or cracked
Probe MAS module turbine worn
diagnostics: Check bearing gas pressure (300–400 kPa) and drive gas pressure (100–200 kPa)
Inspect rotor for chips or cracks
Verify sample packing is even and symmetric
Test at lower spinning speed — if stable, gas pressure or balance is the issue
Check inline gas filter for moisture or oil contamination
corrective_actions: Increase bearing gas pressure to upper range
Repack rotor evenly and use rotor caps correctly
Replace damaged rotor
Purge gas lines and replace inline filter
Contact Bruker service if probe turbines are worn
escalation_conditions: Rotor ejects during experiment — stop immediately, inspect probe and rotor; contact Bruker service before restarting

symptom: Probe cannot be tuned to resonance; reflection coefficient too high; poor RF power transfer
likely_causes: High-dielectric sample (high salt, water) detuning resonance circuit
Probe circuit capacitor or coil damaged
Wrong probe for the nucleus or frequency
RF cable connection loose or damaged
diagnostics: Use wobble function in TopSpin (wobb command): observe tuning curve — dip should be sharp, centered on the operating frequency, and > 20 dB deep; shallow or absent dip indicates circuit mismatch

Compare tuning with and without sample loaded in the rotor: if probe tunes well with empty rotor but not with sample, the dielectric constant of the sample is detuning the circuit — high-water or high-salt samples are common culprits
Test RF cable continuity and VSWR (voltage standing wave ratio) with a cable tester or network analyzer: VSWR > 2:1 indicates cable damage requiring replacement
Try reference sample (adamantane packed in the same rotor) — if adamantane tunes and acquires normally, the issue is sample-specific dielectric loading, not probe hardware failure

Check tune and match capacitor mechanical range: if capacitors are at their mechanical limits (fully in or fully out) and still cannot reach resonance, the dielectric load exceeds the probe tuning range
Inspect probe RF connector for damage, corrosion, or moisture: contaminated connectors cause impedance mismatch that prevents tuning — clean with IPA and compressed air
Test on a different MAS probe if available: if the second probe tunes normally with the same sample, the first probe has a circuit fault

Check that the correct preamp gain and cable routing are being used: some multi-channel probes require specific routing for ¹H vs. X-nucleus channels — incorrect routing causes apparent tuning failure
corrective_actions: Adjust tune and match capacitors to compensate for dielectric loading — for high-dielectric samples, both tune and match may need significant adjustment from normal position; record new positions for future runs with similar samples
For high-salt samples: reduce salt concentration if possible, or use specialized E-field-free probe designs (e.g., Bruker Low-E or Revolution NMR) that are less sensitive to conductive sample loading
Replace RF cable if failed continuity test or VSWR > 2:1 — use Bruker-specified cable type and length to maintain correct impedance matching
Contact Bruker service if probe circuit component has failed — capacitor arcing, coil shorts, and balun failures all require professional repair
For borderline tuning: reduce sample fill volume to 50–75% of full rotor capacity — less sample means less dielectric loading, at the cost of reduced sensitivity
After probe repair or sample change: always re-optimize tune/match and verify with a nutation curve (90° pulse calibration) before acquiring data — incorrect tuning causes severe sensitivity loss
escalation_conditions: Probe cannot be tuned with reference sample — probe circuit fault; contact Bruker NMR service

symptom: Poor signal-to-noise in ssNMR spectrum; excessive signal averaging required; CP efficiency lower than expected
likely_causes: CP contact time not optimized — too short or too long reduces efficiency
Hartmann-Hahn mismatch between ¹H and X channels
Smaller rotor than maximum available for the probe
Recycle delay too short — ¹H T1 not complete between scans
diagnostics: Record CP contact time array — find maximum signal
Run Hartmann-Hahn check with adamantane
Measure ¹H T1 with saturation recovery — use delay of 3–5 × T1
Verify sample fully packed in rotor
corrective_actions: Optimize CP contact time with variable contact time experiment
Recalibrate Hartmann-Hahn match using adamantane
Increase recycle delay for full ¹H T1 recovery
Pack rotor fully using funnel and packing tool
Use larger rotor format if probe supports it
escalation_conditions: Sensitivity unacceptable even after optimization — sample may require isotope labeling

symptom: Audible clicking from probe during experiment; RF artifacts in data; probe protection circuit trips
likely_causes: RF voltage exceeds dielectric breakdown threshold at high power
Moisture inside probe lowering breakdown threshold
Damaged probe capacitor or coil
Long high-power decoupling pulses
diagnostics: Listen for clicking or popping from probe during high-power pulse sequences (CP, decoupling): arcing produces audible clicks at the pulse repetition rate — immediately reduce power or stop experiment to prevent probe damage

Reduce RF power systematically: run experiment at 50%, 70%, and 100% of target power — if arcing occurs only above a specific threshold, that threshold defines the safe operating limit for the current probe condition

Check probe for moisture: condition in dry nitrogen (10 L/min flow through probe body) for 4–12 hours — moisture dramatically lowers dielectric breakdown threshold, especially in MAS probes where centrifugal force distributes moisture onto coil surfaces

Examine probe protection circuit logs in TopSpin (probehead protection or HPPR status): recorded events show when and how frequently protection activated — frequent trips indicate chronic issue requiring service
Check RF pulse duration and duty cycle: long high-power pulses (> 200 µs at high power) or high duty cycle sequences (e.g., CW decoupling during long acquisition) are most likely to cause arcing
Monitor reflected power during pulsing: high reflected power (> 10% of forward power) indicates impedance mismatch that concentrates voltage at specific circuit points, promoting dielectric breakdown

Inspect probe for visible damage after removing from magnet: scorch marks, discolored capacitors, or melted insulation indicate previous arcing damage that weakens the probe and lowers the arcing threshold

Test arcing threshold with a dummy rotor containing adamantane (low dielectric) vs. sample — if arcing occurs only with sample, the sample dielectric properties are contributing to the breakdown condition
corrective_actions: Reduce RF power to minimum required for experiment: for ¹H decoupling, target γB1/2π ≈ 50–80 kHz instead of > 100 kHz — lower power with TPPM or SPINAL decoupling achieves similar line narrowing
Dry probe with nitrogen purge overnight (12 hours minimum, 5–10 L/min flow) — critical for probes stored in humid environments or after aqueous sample runs
Use TPPM or SPINAL-64 decoupling instead of high-power CW decoupling — TPPM achieves equivalent line narrowing at 30–50% lower average power, reducing arcing risk significantly

Contact Bruker NMR service immediately if arcing persists after power reduction and drying — arcing can permanently damage probe capacitors, coils, and balun transformers; continued operation risks catastrophic probe failure
After arcing event: re-calibrate 90° pulse on adamantane — arcing may have changed probe circuit characteristics, altering the effective B1 field
Implement a probe drying protocol: purge with dry N2 for 30 min before each session and maintain N2 flow during non-use periods in humid climates
escalation_conditions: Arcing recurs after power reduction and drying — probe requires professional inspection before further use

symptom: NMR field lock lost or cannot be established; field stability poor; spectrum shows broadened or shifted peaks
likely_causes: Insufficient deuterium signal — wrong solvent or non-deuterated solvent
Severely degraded shimming preventing lock
Sample tube not centered in spinner
Incorrect lock channel parameters
Lock amplifier or channel hardware fault
diagnostics: Check lock display — observe signal level and correction output
Verify sample solvent is deuterated (> 99.5% D)
Center tube in spinner gauge before insertion
Try automatic lock search in TopSpin — if found but unstable, shimming is the issue
corrective_actions: Use correct deuterated solvent (D₂O, CDCl₃, DMSO-d6)
Align sample depth with spinner gauge reference mark
Run automatic shim (topshim or sampleshim) to restore lock stability
Re-set lock phase using lock display panel
Contact Bruker service if lock channel hardware fault suspected
escalation_conditions: Lock cannot be obtained with standard CDCl₃ — lock channel hardware fault; contact Bruker NMR service

symptom: NMR peaks broader than expected; asymmetric lineshape; reference peak (TMS/DSS) has poor shape
likely_causes: Paramagnetic contaminants in sample — trace metals
Low-quality or damaged NMR tube
Shim settings not optimized for current sample
Temperature gradient in sample volume
Dissolved oxygen (paramagnetic)
diagnostics: Measure ¹H linewidth of TMS or DSS — should be < 1 Hz for good shimming
Inspect tube for scratches or deformation
Check for paramagnetic contamination
Run gradient shimming (topshim 3D)
corrective_actions: Run gradient shim (topshim 3D) to optimize shim map
Use high-quality precision NMR tubes (Wilmad 528-PP or equivalent)
Degas sample or sparge with nitrogen to remove dissolved oxygen
Chelate metal ions with 1–5 mM EDTA if paramagnetic contamination suspected
escalation_conditions: Cannot achieve < 5 Hz linewidth with standard sample — magnet shim coil fault; contact Bruker service immediately

symptom: Solvent peak not adequately suppressed; residual solvent overwhelms analyte peaks or creates baseline artifacts
likely_causes: Presaturation frequency not exactly on solvent resonance
Water T1 too long for presaturation to achieve > 99% saturation
Analyte concentration too low relative to partially suppressed solvent
WATERGATE or excitation sculpting 90° pulse miscalibrated
Temperature drift shifting solvent frequency
diagnostics: Confirm O1 is exactly on solvent frequency using a quick 1D ¹H spectrum without solvent suppression: measure solvent peak position in Hz and set O1 to that exact value — offset of even 5 Hz degrades presaturation efficiency

Check presaturation power (PLW9 or equivalent): optimal power produces ~25 Hz γB1 field — too high (> 50 Hz) causes radiation damping and Bloch-Siegert shifts; too low (< 10 Hz) is ineffective for T1-dependent saturation
Verify 90° pulse calibration is current for WATERGATE experiments: incorrect 90° pulse causes incomplete inversion in the binomial sequence, degrading suppression by 10–100×

Check sample temperature stability: temperature fluctuation shifts solvent resonance frequency (water moves ~5 Hz/°C at 400 MHz), causing presaturation to miss the target — stabilize temperature to ±0.1 °C

Run presaturation with different saturation times (1, 2, 3, 5 s) and compare residual solvent peak: plot residual intensity vs. saturation time — optimal time depends on water T1 (~3 s in protein solutions, > 5 s in pure water)
Verify receiver gain is appropriate: if gain is set based on the unsuppressed solvent peak, it may be too high for the suppressed spectrum, causing ADC clipping and baseline artifacts
Check for radiation damping in concentrated water samples: presaturation at too high B1 drives radiation damping that actively opposes saturation — reduce power and increase duration instead

Compare multiple suppression schemes on the same sample: presaturation, WATERGATE W5, excitation sculpting (zgesgp), and WET — different schemes have different suppression bandwidths and baseline characteristics
corrective_actions: Set O1 exactly to solvent frequency using 1D spectrum — re-check O1 at the beginning of each session and after any temperature change
Increase presaturation duration to 2–5 s for water suppression — extend to 5–8 s for samples with long water T1 (dilute aqueous solutions without paramagnetic additives)
Optimize presaturation power with array experiment: run PLW9 from 1 to 100 dB attenuation and select the power level giving minimum residual water signal

Switch to WATERGATE W5 or excitation sculpting (zgesgp) for better suppression bandwidth and flatter baseline near solvent — these methods are preferred for samples with peaks near the water resonance
Recalibrate 90° pulse before solvent-suppressed experiments: use pulsecal or manual nutation curve — 90° pulse typically 8–15 µs at 400 MHz depending on probe
Set receiver gain after solvent suppression is active: use rga (automatic receiver gain adjustment) with the suppression sequence running — prevents ADC overflow artifacts
For biological samples in 90% H2O/10% D2O: consider adding 0.02% NaN3 and 50 µM DSS as reference — NaN3 prevents microbial growth during long acquisitions
escalation_conditions: Solvent suppression failure across all schemes — receiver dynamic range limitation; consider deuterated solvent

symptom: NMR peaks broader than expected; insufficient resolution to observe multiplicity or coupling constants
likely_causes: Paramagnetic contamination — trace metal ions cause dramatic broadening
High molecular weight — slow tumbling broadens peaks
Chemical exchange at intermediate rate on NMR timescale
Poor shimming
Protein or oligonucleotide aggregation
diagnostics: Measure ¹H linewidth on TMS or DSS reference — distinguishes shimming from sample issues
Add EDTA chelator — if peaks sharpen, paramagnetic metals present
Measure at different temperatures — peaks sharpen at higher T if slow-tumbling or exchange
Check sample by DLS for aggregation
corrective_actions: Add 1–5 mM EDTA to chelate trace metals
Prepare samples in metal-free water with HNO3-cleaned tubes
Measure at higher temperature (310 K) for macromolecules
Degas sample to remove dissolved oxygen
Re-shim before measurement
escalation_conditions: Peaks remain broad after EDTA and temperature optimization — consider isotope labeling or cryoprobe

symptom: Gradient-based experiments (HSQC, HMBC, diffusion NMR) fail to produce expected correlations; artifacts in 2D spectra
likely_causes: Gradient amplifier fault or not connected
Gradient calibration outdated
Incorrect gradient pulse amplitude in pulse program
Metallic NMR tube accessories near gradient coil
diagnostics: Run gradcal in TopSpin to measure gradient strength: diffusion coefficient of doped water (1% H2O in D2O with 0.1 mg/mL GdCl3) should give D = 1.9 × 10⁻⁹ m²/s at 25 °C — deviation > 10% indicates gradient calibration error
Check gradient amplifier status in TopSpin hardware check window (eda or edacq): verify amplifier responds to test pulse without fault — amber/red status indicates hardware fault
Verify gradient cable connection at probe head: gradient coil cable should be firmly connected with clean pins — corrosion or loose connectors cause intermittent gradient failures
Test HSQC on standard compound (sucrose or menthol in CDCl3): absence of expected cross-peaks while 1D spectra are normal confirms gradient failure

Run 1D gradient echo experiment (e.g., pulse-gradient spin echo, PGSE): if echo is not refocused, gradient pulse is not being applied correctly — verify gradient pulse amplitude and shape in the pulse program

Check for eddy current artifacts: acquire gradient echo with variable gradient recovery delay (50 µs to 5 ms) — persistent signal distortion at short delays indicates eddy currents requiring pre-emphasis adjustment
Monitor gradient coil temperature during high-duty-cycle experiments (diffusion DOSY): overheated gradient coil causes automatic shutdown — verify cooling airflow to probe gradient region
Test with a simple gradient experiment (e.g., 1D gradient-selected ¹H with single gradient pulse) before running complex 2D experiments — isolates gradient hardware from pulse program issues
corrective_actions: Recalibrate gradient using diffusion measurement of doped water standard: update gradient calibration constant in TopSpin (GPNAM parameters) based on measured vs. expected diffusion coefficient
Reseat gradient cable connections at probe: clean connector pins with IPA and lint-free tissue, ensure firm connection without forcing — overtightening can damage connector threads
Power cycle gradient amplifier: turn off amplifier, wait 30 s, turn on — some amplifier faults are cleared by power cycle; persistent faults require service
Use standard glass NMR tubes only near gradient coil: metallic spinner components or tube caps near the gradient coil create eddy currents that distort gradient pulses
Contact Bruker service if amplifier hardware fault confirmed — do not attempt internal amplifier repair; gradient amplifiers operate at high current (up to 30 A)
After gradient repair or recalibration: verify performance with HSQC on sucrose standard and compare cross-peak pattern to reference dataset
For diffusion experiments (DOSY): calibrate gradient strength independently using a sample with known diffusion coefficient (e.g., HDO, D = 1.9 × 10⁻⁹ m²/s at 25 °C) before measuring unknown samples
escalation_conditions: Gradient calibration fails on standard — gradient amplifier or coil fault; contact Bruker service

symptom: System pressure alarm — pump unable to reach target flow rate; pressure rapidly increases to cutoff
likely_causes: blocked inline filter on the pressure sensor (KNAUER proprietary part)
clogged HPLC column or guard column
worn or swollen pump head seals causing reduced bore diameter
faulty check valves (KNAUER dual-piston: inlet or outlet check valve)
blocked frit in solvent filter or inlet tubing
mobile phase precipitation at low temperature
diagnostics: Disconnect column and measure pressure at same flow rate — high pressure without column indicates pump or tubing issue; normal system pressure without column is typically < 30 bar at 1 mL/min
Replace the inline pressure sensor filter (KNAUER part) every 3–6 months as routine maintenance — this small sintered filter is frequently the hidden source of high pressure on KNAUER systems

Open KNAUER ServiceTool (or ClarityChrom diagnostics) and record pump pressure profile to identify check valve malfunction — normal profile shows smooth sinusoidal waves; sharp spikes indicate check valve leak-back
Inspect inlet solvent filter under the solvent reservoir — replace if discoloured or >6 months old; a blocked inlet filter causes cavitation and erratic pressure rather than steady high pressure
Inspect tubing for kinks, blockages, or incorrect fitting compression — even a slight overtightening of PEEK ferrules on 1/16 inch OD tubing can collapse the ID

Measure pressure at multiple flow rates (0.2, 0.5, 1.0 mL/min) and plot pressure vs. flow: a linear relationship indicates normal flow resistance; non-linear suggests partial blockage becoming flow-dependent
Check guard column separately from analytical column: disconnect guard, measure pressure, then reconnect — guard columns clog first and are cheap to replace
Verify mobile phase is fully dissolved and filtered: inspect visually for cloudiness; re-filter through 0.22 µm PTFE membrane if any doubt about particulate content
corrective_actions: Replace inline pressure sensor filter (Part No. A4949) and reset pressure alarm before restarting — keep spare filters in stock as they require replacement every 3–6 months
Flush column or replace guard column; if pressure remains > 20% above initial column pressure after guard replacement, replace analytical column
Replace check valves (inlet and outlet) for the affected pump head — sonicate old check valves in IPA as a temporary fix if new valves are not immediately available
Replace pump head seals (piston seals + back-piston seals) per KNAUER seal replacement procedure — use only KNAUER OEM seals to maintain pressure rating
Use fresh-filtered, degassed mobile phase; warm solvents to room temperature before use — buffer solutions prepared cold may precipitate as they warm in the system
If issue persists after all above, run KNAUER Pump P 2.1S/P 4.1S Instructions (V6870) leak pressure test to identify internal pump head leakage
For buffer methods: establish an end-of-day flush protocol — flush with 100% water for 15 min, then 50% methanol/water for 15 min to prevent salt crystallization overnight
escalation_conditions: Pressure alarm persists after column removal and filter replacement — seal or check valve replacement required
ServiceTool shows irregular pressure profile in both pistons — pump head replacement needed; contact KNAUER service
SAFETY: Do not disconnect fittings while system is pressurized above 50 bar — always stop pump and wait for pressure to drop to zero before loosening any fitting

symptom: Detector signal weak or absent; baseline unusually high; lamp intensity warning in ClarityChrom/knauerOS
likely_causes: aging deuterium lamp (> 1500 hours or > 2 years)
dirty or contaminated UV flow cell (salt deposits, UV-absorbing residue)
incorrect wavelength programmed or wrong flow cell selected in software
damaged optical fiber or loose fiber connector in DAD 2.1L
mobile phase highly UV-absorbing at selected wavelength
diagnostics: Check lamp hours in knauerOS or ClarityChrom diagnostics panel — KNAUER recommends replacement after 1500–2000 hours; note the cumulative hours and compare to last qualification result
Run a solvent blank: compare absorbance baseline to expected value for your mobile phase at selected wavelength — baseline should be < 0.5 AU at 254 nm with methanol/water (50:50)
Inspect flow cell for visible deposits; check if cleaning with 0.1 M HNO3 flush improves signal — observe whether baseline drops by > 0.1 AU after cleaning
For DAD 2.1L: perform wavelength calibration check using holmium oxide standard built into the instrument — peaks at 241.1, 287.6, 361.5 nm should be within ±1 nm

Measure signal-to-noise ratio by injecting known concentration standard (e.g., 10 µg/mL caffeine at 272 nm) and compare S/N to historical qualification data — S/N decrease > 50% confirms sensitivity loss
Check optical fiber coupling at both detector and lamp housing ends — loose connections reduce light throughput by up to 80%; gently tighten finger-tight
Verify the correct flow cell is installed for the application: standard analytical (10 mm path), semi-micro (6 mm), or prep (0.5 mm) — wrong cell drastically changes sensitivity
Run lamp energy test from knauerOS diagnostics: compare D2 lamp output intensity at 254 nm against factory specification — output below 50% of initial indicates imminent failure
corrective_actions: Replace deuterium lamp (KNAUER Part No. A4290) and run lamp burn-in procedure per V6872 manual — allow 30 min burn-in before any measurements to stabilize output
Clean UV flow cell: flush with 50% MeOH / 50% 0.1 M HNO3 for 10 min, then flush with water, then MeOH — for protein residue, use 6 M guanidine HCl flush first
Verify detector wavelength settings match your analyte absorption maximum — use analyte UV spectrum to select optimal wavelength for maximum response
If DAD 2.1L: reseat fiber connectors by unscrewing, cleaning fiber ends with lens tissue and IPA, then retightening — re-run holmium oxide calibration to verify wavelength accuracy
Switch to a mobile phase with lower UV background (e.g., LC-MS grade solvents or lower acetate/formate concentration) — TFA absorbs strongly below 220 nm, consider switching to formic acid
After lamp replacement, run full detector qualification: noise, drift, linearity (5-point caffeine or naphthalene), and wavelength accuracy tests per KNAUER IQ/OQ/PQ protocol
For persistent sensitivity loss after lamp and cell maintenance: replace the reference diode if available on the AZURA UVD model — degraded reference causes apparent sensitivity loss
escalation_conditions: Signal does not recover after lamp replacement and flow cell cleaning — fiber or detector optics damage; contact KNAUER service
Wavelength calibration with holmium oxide deviates > 2 nm from certified values — optical alignment required by KNAUER service engineer
SAFETY: Deuterium lamp emits UV radiation — never look directly at operating lamp without UV-protective eyewear; always close lamp housing before operating detector

symptom: Residual peaks from previous injection appear in blank runs; carryover > 0.1% of peak area
likely_causes: insufficient needle wash volume or wash solvent too weak for analyte
blocked or partially clogged needle wash port
injection valve internal leakage (rotor seal wear)
inadequate flush of sample loop between injections
sample adsorption onto stainless steel needle or loop
diagnostics: Run blank injection immediately after high-concentration sample and calculate carryover % — carryover = (blank peak area / sample peak area) × 100; acceptable is typically < 0.1% for quantitative methods
Check needle wash program in ClarityChrom/knauerOS — verify wash volume (> 3x loop volume) and wash solvent polarity matches the analyte solubility characteristics
Inspect needle wash port for blockage or residue — remove the wash port cap and flush with 50% methanol using a syringe to clear any accumulated sample residue
Run needle wash step with stronger solvent (100% organic) and monitor if carryover decreases — test sequentially with MeOH, ACN, then DMSO to find effective wash solvent

Check injection valve rotor seal condition: inject 1 µL of colored dye (e.g., 0.1% methylene blue) and inspect the valve seat area for leakage past the rotor seal — visible dye around the seal indicates wear
Verify sample loop flush volume in the method — partial loop injections require > 5× loop volume flush to eliminate dead volume carryover
Test whether carryover is analyte-specific: run the same test with a non-adsorptive standard (e.g., caffeine) — if no carryover with caffeine, the issue is analyte adsorption on metal surfaces
Inspect the autosampler needle tip under magnification — bent or burred needle tips cause incomplete wipe-off at the needle seat, leading to persistent carryover
corrective_actions: Increase needle wash volume to 5x sample loop volume — program a multi-step wash cycle: strong organic first (100% ACN), then intermediate (50% MeOH/water), then initial mobile phase composition
Use a two-step wash: strong organic solvent then weak aqueous solvent (matches mobile phase start conditions) — ensure dwell time in wash solvent is at least 5 seconds for effective contact
Replace injection valve rotor seal (KNAUER rotor seal kit for AS 6.1L) if leakage is suspected — follow KNAUER AS 6.1L rotor seal replacement procedure exactly, torque to specification
For basic compounds: add 0.1% ammonium hydroxide to needle wash solvent to prevent adsorption on stainless steel surfaces — basic analytes (amines, peptides) adsorb strongly to metal
Switch to PEEK needle/loop for biological samples if stainless steel adsorption is suspected — PEEK is inert to proteins and peptides
For acidic compounds or metal chelators: add 0.05% EDTA to the needle wash to prevent analyte-metal coordination on stainless steel surfaces
If carryover persists at the injection valve, perform a full valve disassembly and cleaning: sonicate rotor and stator in 50% IPA for 15 min, dry with nitrogen, and reassemble with new rotor seal
escalation_conditions: Carryover > 1% after wash optimisation and valve rotor seal replacement — possible internal surface contamination requiring full autosampler service
SAFETY: When handling needle wash solvents containing organic solvents or ammonium hydroxide, work in a well-ventilated area and wear appropriate gloves (nitrile for organic solvents)

symptom: Retention times drifting or shifting over multiple runs despite identical method conditions
likely_causes: column thermostat not equilibrated — CT 2.1 requires ~15 min at target temperature
laboratory ambient temperature fluctuation affecting un-thermostated pre-column tubing
Peltier element malfunction or temperature setpoint not reached (CT 2.1 range: 5–85 °C)
column aging or silanol activity changes
mobile phase composition drift (improper mixing or degassing)
diagnostics: Monitor CT 2.1 actual temperature readout in knauerOS before starting batch — confirm setpoint is reached and stable within ±0.1 °C for at least 5 minutes before injecting
Check retention time stability over 6–10 isocratic injections at the start of each day — RT RSD should be < 0.3% for isocratic methods and < 0.5% for gradient methods
Verify mobile phase is freshly prepared and degassed — compare pH (within ±0.05 of target), conductivity, and organic:aqueous ratio to previous qualifying batch
Run column equilibration with at least 10 column volumes at start conditions before any injection — for gradient methods, run 2–3 blank gradients to pre-condition the column
Measure pump flow rate accuracy by gravimetric method: collect 10 min of eluent, weigh on 3-decimal balance — actual flow should be within ±1% of setpoint
Compare column backpressure to the value recorded when the column was new — pressure increase > 20% indicates partial frit blockage or column degradation that can shift RT
Check gradient delay volume (dwell volume) by injecting unretained marker with and without gradient — dwell volume changes from plumbing modifications shift gradient-eluted peak RTs
Review system suitability data for RT trend over the past 50 injections — gradual drift indicates column aging; sudden shift indicates mobile phase or hardware change
corrective_actions: Allow CT 2.1 to equilibrate for minimum 20 min before starting analysis — verify both set and actual temperature match on knauerOS display
Insulate pre-column tubing from ambient temperature changes — use foam tubing insulation or route tubing through the column oven
Verify temperature setpoint is not exceeding column stationary phase specification (e.g., max 60 °C for standard silica C18, max 80 °C for BEH chemistry)
If Peltier malfunction suspected: run temperature verification test in knauerOS diagnostics with an external calibrated thermometer as reference
Prepare fresh mobile phase: weigh buffer salts on calibrated balance, verify pH with recently calibrated pH meter, filter through 0.22 µm, and degas before use
If RT shifts correlate with column pressure increase: flush column in reverse direction with strong organic solvent per manufacturer instructions to clear accumulated matrix at inlet frit
Re-determine gradient delay volume after any plumbing change: inject acetone tracer with step gradient from 0% to 100% B and measure delay between program step and UV response
escalation_conditions: Temperature setpoint not reached after equilibration — Peltier module fault; contact KNAUER service
RT drift > 2% persists after fresh mobile phase, column equilibration, and temperature stabilization — column degradation; replace column and requalify

symptom: Irregular baseline noise during UV detection — spikes or oscillation at UV detector output
likely_causes: air microbubbles in flow cell caused by dissolved gas in mobile phase
pressure pulsation from pump at low flow rates
loose electrical connection on detector or interface box (IFU 2.1)
contaminated UV flow cell (particulates or film)
mobile phase solvent impurity or UV-absorbing contamination
diagnostics: Switch to degassed HPLC-grade water at 1 mL/min and check if noise disappears — confirms mobile phase origin; baseline noise should be < 0.5 mAU peak-to-peak at 254 nm for a clean system
Check pump pressure trace in knauerOS diagnostics: if pulsation amplitude > 2% of mean pressure, check piston seal condition and verify pump damper is functioning correctly
Inspect all electrical connections between detector and IFU 2.1 interface box — loose connectors cause intermittent noise spikes that appear random; reseat all D-sub and USB connections firmly
Flush flow cell with 50% methanol/water for 5 min and reassess baseline — persistent noise after flushing suggests contaminated flow cell windows requiring HNO3 treatment

Measure baseline noise at multiple wavelengths (210, 254, 280, 350 nm): noise that increases dramatically below 230 nm indicates mobile phase purity issue; noise constant across wavelengths indicates electronic or air bubble origin
Check online degasser function: verify degasser vacuum pump is audible; test by comparing baseline noise with and without degasser — degasser failure is a common hidden cause of baseline spikes
Inspect for leaks at all post-pump fittings using tissue paper — even micro-leaks introduce air into the flow path, causing periodic baseline spikes that coincide with pump strokes
Record baseline noise power spectrum if ClarityChrom supports it — noise at pump stroke frequency (typically 0.5–2 Hz for dual-piston pumps) confirms pump-origin pulsation
corrective_actions: Use online degasser — ensure all channels are active and vacuum pump is running; replace degasser membrane if vacuum level is insufficient (typical target: < 100 mbar internal)
Replace mobile phase with freshly degassed HPLC-grade solvents — open new bottles for each batch; old solvents absorb atmospheric gases over days
Clean UV flow cell per KNAUER UVD maintenance procedure: flush with 0.1 M HNO3 for 5 min, then water for 5 min, then methanol for 5 min — repeat if baseline does not improve
Check and reseat detector-to-IFU 2.1 cable connection — if cable shows wear, replace with KNAUER OEM cable to ensure proper shielding
At low flow rates (< 0.3 mL/min): enable pulse damper and increase detector time constant (response time) to smooth out pump pulsation artifacts
Replace pump piston seals if noise correlates with pump stroke frequency — KNAUER recommends seal replacement every 6–12 months depending on mobile phase aggressiveness
Install a backpressure restrictor (50–100 psi) after the detector to keep dissolved gases in solution through the flow cell
escalation_conditions: Noise spike pattern is systematic (every N seconds) — piston seal or check valve failure; replace seals
Baseline noise > 5 mAU peak-to-peak at 254 nm after all corrections — UV lamp or photodiode degradation; contact KNAUER service

symptom: ClarityChrom or knauerOS cannot detect or communicate with AZURA instrument modules on LAN or RS-232
likely_causes: incorrect IP address assignment — AZURA modules default to DHCP; fixed IP required for stable ClarityChrom communication
network switch or firewall blocking KNAUER communication port 10001
incompatible ClarityChrom driver version for the installed AZURA firmware version
IFU 2.1 interface box USB driver not installed or not recognised by Windows
RS-232 cable connected to wrong COM port or baud rate mismatch
diagnostics: Ping the AZURA module IP address from the ClarityChrom PC — if no response, check LAN cable, network switch port LED, and verify PC and module are on the same subnet
Open KNAUER Configuration Manager and check if module is listed and shows green status — red or absent modules indicate communication failure at the network or driver level
Check AZURA front display for IP address and compare with ClarityChrom configuration — mismatch between displayed IP and configured IP is the most common cause of detection failure
Check Windows Device Manager for IFU 2.1 USB device — yellow warning icon indicates driver issue; right-click and select Update Driver to attempt automatic fix
Verify network switch port is active: connect a laptop directly to the same switch port and confirm connectivity — dead switch ports are a frequent overlooked cause
Test with a crossover or direct LAN cable between PC and AZURA module — bypasses the switch to isolate switch-related issues
Check if Windows Firewall or antivirus is blocking KNAUER communication port 10001 — temporarily disable firewall and test; if communication succeeds, add port exception permanently
Review ClarityChrom event log (Help > Diagnostics > Event Log) for specific communication timeout error codes — error codes reference KNAUER troubleshooting guide chapter 7
corrective_actions: Assign fixed static IP to each AZURA module via the front panel menu — use a dedicated subnet (e.g., 192.168.10.x) for all KNAUER instruments to avoid lab network conflicts
Allow KNAUER communication port 10001 (TCP/UDP) through Windows Firewall — create both inbound and outbound rules for the ClarityChrom executable and port 10001
Update ClarityChrom KNAUER driver pack to match AZURA module firmware version — download from KNAUER website (knauer.net) and verify version compatibility in the release notes
Reinstall IFU 2.1 USB driver from KNAUER website — uninstall existing driver first, reboot, then install fresh driver before reconnecting USB cable
Restart all AZURA modules and relaunch ClarityChrom after network configuration changes — power-cycle modules in correct sequence: pump last, detector first
If RS-232 connection: verify COM port number in Windows Device Manager matches ClarityChrom configuration; set baud rate to 9600 (KNAUER default) and verify cable pinout
escalation_conditions: Module shows IP conflict or cannot be configured via front panel — factory reset required per KNAUER service
Communication fails after driver reinstall and direct cable test — internal communication board fault on AZURA module; contact KNAUER service for hardware diagnosis

symptom: Pressure alarm at 1000 bar cutoff; system stops mid-run on AZURA UHPLC platform
likely_causes: sub-2 µm column frit clogging from sample matrix particulates
mobile phase precipitation at high pressure
inadequate sample filtration (particles > 0.2 µm entering column)
pump seal deterioration causing high-pressure fluctuations
column temperature too low — increasing mobile phase viscosity
diagnostics: Remove column and measure system pressure at same flow rate; > 50 bar without column indicates pump/tubing issue
Replace guard column first and retest before replacing analytical column
Verify sample is filtered through 0.2 µm filter or centrifuged at > 13 000 rpm
Check column temperature setting — 40–60 °C reduces backpressure significantly
corrective_actions: Replace guard column frit or cartridge first; if pressure persists, replace analytical column
Filter all samples through 0.2 µm syringe filter before injection
Increase column temperature to 40 °C to reduce mobile phase viscosity
Reduce flow rate by 10–20% and reassess peak performance
Replace UHPLC pump seals annually or every 5000 hours per KNAUER P 2.1L schedule
escalation_conditions: Pressure exceeds cutoff within first column volume of any new column — column failure; contact KNAUER

symptom: Peak efficiency significantly below specification for sub-2 µm columns on KNAUER UHPLC
likely_causes: extra-column band broadening from overlong or large-bore connecting tubing (must use < 0.1 mm ID for UHPLC)
large injection volume exceeding 10% of first peak volume for sub-2 µm columns
strong sample solvent (stronger than mobile phase A) causing peak distortion
poor column equilibration — UHPLC columns require > 20 column volumes
diagnostics: Inject a standard compound with known plate count and compare against vendor datasheet — calculate N = 5.54 × (tR/W1/2)²; plates should be > 70% of certificate value for a column in good condition
Check tubing ID from injector to column inlet — must be 0.075–0.12 mm ID for UHPLC; standard HPLC tubing (0.17 mm ID) causes catastrophic band broadening for sub-2 µm columns
Reduce injection volume to 1–2 µL and compare peak shape — plot plate count vs injection volume; efficiency loss > 10% indicates injection volume is too large
Check sample solvent strength — should be at or below mobile phase A composition; injecting in 100% organic onto a C18 column at high aqueous initial conditions causes severe peak distortion

Measure extra-column volume: replace column with zero-dead-volume union, inject uracil at 0.4 mL/min — peak variance should be < 3 µL² (corresponding to < 5 µL peak width at 4σ) for proper UHPLC performance

Inspect all fittings from injector to detector for correct ferrule type: UHPLC requires zero-dead-volume fittings (e.g., Waters Viper, IDEX MarvelX) — standard finger-tight fittings may contribute > 1 µL dead volume per connection
Verify detector flow cell volume is appropriate: UHPLC requires ≤ 500 nL (micro) flow cell; standard 13 µL analytical flow cells cause major band broadening for narrow UHPLC peaks
Check detector data acquisition rate — for peaks < 3 seconds wide, acquisition rate should be ≥ 20 Hz (50 ms response time) to capture peak shape accurately
corrective_actions: Replace all post-injector tubing with 0.075 mm ID PEEK or stainless steel tubing — cut to minimum length needed; every extra centimeter adds extra-column volume
Reduce injection volume to ≤ 2 µL for a 2.1 × 50 mm column and ≤ 5 µL for a 2.1 × 100 mm column — use higher concentration samples to compensate if needed
Dissolve sample in weak solvent (mobile phase A or weaker) — this ensures analyte focuses at the column head during injection
Equilibrate column with ≥ 20 column volumes at initial gradient conditions before injection — insufficient equilibration is the leading cause of first-injection peak broadening
Install zero-dead-volume fittings throughout the post-injector flow path: use Viper or MarvelX connectors at column inlet and outlet for consistent sealing without dead volume
Switch to a UHPLC-compatible detector flow cell (≤ 500 nL path volume, 10 mm path length) if currently using standard analytical cell
Increase detector data acquisition rate to ≥ 40 Hz and reduce time constant to ≤ 0.025 s for sub-2-second UHPLC peaks
escalation_conditions: Column plates below 50% of specification after tubing and volume optimisation — column contamination or packing damage; replace column
SAFETY: UHPLC systems operate at pressures up to 1300 bar — never loosen fittings while system is pressurized; always stop pump and depressurize before making any plumbing changes

symptom: Retention times drifting cycle-to-cycle on high-throughput QC workflow; precision RSD > 0.5%
likely_causes: rapid column cycling without adequate re-equilibration between gradients
flow rate accuracy drift at high throughput due to pump wear
temperature equilibration lag between rapid sequential injections
sample carryover from previous injection affecting gradient start
diagnostics: Run 20 consecutive injections of a standard compound and calculate RT RSD — acceptable RT RSD for UHPLC QC methods should be < 0.3% across the sequence
Check pump flow rate accuracy using gravimetric method at the specified QC flow rate — collect eluent for 10 min and weigh; deviation > 0.5% requires recalibration
Verify post-gradient re-equilibration time (minimum 2–3 column volumes) before each injection — for sub-2-µm columns at 0.5 mL/min on a 50 × 2.1 mm column, 1 column volume ≈ 0.1 mL
Monitor column pressure at start of each run — increasing pressure over the sequence indicates progressive frit blockage that correlates with RT drift
