Compare RT trend direction: earlier RT drift suggests column degradation or mobile phase composition change; later RT drift suggests temperature not equilibrated or increasing dead volume
Check mixer volume calibration in knauerOS — for high-throughput rapid gradient methods, even 50 µL mixer volume error significantly shifts gradient-eluted peaks
Measure dwell volume using acetone tracer with step gradient: compare measured dwell volume against the value in the PurityChrom/knauerOS method — mismatch causes systematic RT offset
Verify sample thermostat temperature on the autosampler — cold samples injected into warm column cause transient retention shifts on the first few injections
corrective_actions: Increase post-gradient re-equilibration to at least 5 column volumes for maximum RT reproducibility in high-throughput QC workflows
Run pump qualification (flow rate accuracy) test in knauerOS — recalibrate if > ±0.5% deviation; use the KNAUER gravimetric protocol with degassed water at 20 °C
Increase column thermostat equilibration time or switch to isothermal method — for gradient methods, run 3 conditioning gradients before beginning the sample sequence
Add needle wash between every injection to minimise carryover effects on gradient start — use 3× loop volume of strong wash followed by weak wash
Pre-heat sample tray to column temperature (if method allows) to eliminate thermal mismatch between injected sample and column equilibrium
Replace column inlet frit if pressure trend shows accumulation — install a guard column or in-line filter to protect the analytical column and maintain consistent RT
escalation_conditions: RT RSD > 2% despite re-equilibration — pump seal wear; schedule preventive maintenance
RT shifts abruptly mid-sequence — possible air bubble in pump or mobile phase composition change; check solvent levels and pump priming

symptom: AZURA Bio system pressure exceeds column specification (max 240 bar); run aborted
likely_causes: air in biocompatible pump head causing pressure spikes
clogged column frit from precipitated protein or aggregated sample
incorrect tubing ID for high-flow bio applications
buffer salt precipitation in capillaries at low temperature
pump seal contamination from sample matrix
diagnostics: Prime AZURA Bio pump with degassed buffer (minimum 5 mL) before connecting column
Disconnect column and measure system dead volume pressure at target flow rate in PurityChrom
Inspect all PEEK/titanium fittings for blockages
Check column pressure log — identify whether pressure rises from run start or during gradient
corrective_actions: Prime both pump channels thoroughly with degassed buffer before each use
Wash column with 5 column volumes of 20% ethanol/water to dissolve protein aggregates on frit
Replace column inlet frit if pressure remains high after wash
Use 0.75–1.0 mm ID tubing for flows > 10 mL/min
Filter all samples through 0.22 µm membrane before loading onto column
escalation_conditions: Column pressure does not decrease after washing — column frit or column replacement required

symptom: Noisy UV baseline at 280 nm during protein purification run on AZURA Bio system
likely_causes: air microbubbles in biocompatible UV flow cell when switching between high-salt and low-salt buffers
refractive index change during gradient causing apparent UV signal change
protein aggregates passing through flow cell
incorrect reference wavelength setting
buffer gradient composition causing UV-absorbing baseline
diagnostics: Run UV baseline scan in PurityChrom with column bypassed and buffer flowing
Check reference wavelength: set to 360 nm when measuring at 280 nm to compensate refractive index changes
Degas both buffer A and buffer B before use
Compare UV trace at 280 nm vs 254 nm — if both noisy, likely flow cell contamination
corrective_actions: Degas all buffers by vacuum filtration (0.22 µm membrane + vacuum) before use
Set UV reference wavelength to 360 nm to compensate gradient refractive index changes
Flush UV flow cell with 50% ethanol / 50% water for 5 min, then equilibrate with buffer A
Filter sample through 0.22 µm before loading to remove aggregates
Reduce gradient slope to minimise refractive index change rate
escalation_conditions: Baseline noise > 5 mAU after degassing and flow cell flush — UV cell contamination; clean with 0.1 M NaOH flush

symptom: Protein peaks poorly resolved in SEC run; aggregate and monomer peaks overlapping
likely_causes: flow rate too high for SEC column (SEC resolution decreases above 0.5 mL/min for 300 mm columns)
injection volume too large — > 2% of column volume causes peak broadening in SEC
column void volume increased (column settling or void at top)
sample protein concentration too high causing viscous fingering
incorrect mobile phase ionic strength (< 50 mM salt causes non-specific ionic interactions)
diagnostics: Check injection volume as percentage of column volume — should be < 1.5% for optimal SEC resolution
Run molecular weight standards at half the method flow rate and compare resolution
Inspect column chromatogram for void volume peak to detect packing issues
Verify mobile phase contains 100–150 mM NaCl or equivalent ionic strength
corrective_actions: Reduce flow rate to 0.3–0.5 mL/min for 300 mm SEC columns
Reduce injection volume to < 1% of column volume
Dilute sample to < 5 mg/mL protein concentration
Prepare mobile phase with 100–150 mM NaCl + 20 mM phosphate pH 7.4 (standard SEC buffer)
If void volume detected: replace SEC column
escalation_conditions: Resolution does not improve after volume and flow rate reduction — column aging or void; replace column

symptom: Gradient elution profile inconsistent between runs; protein elution shifts or step gradient not accurate in PurityChrom
likely_causes: air in gradient mixing chamber or pump head affecting composition accuracy
buffer A or B inlet filter blocked — causing suction instability
pump channel flow rate deviation > 1% causing composition error
delay volume miscalculation in PurityChrom gradient method
PurityChrom method step gradient programmed without hold time at transition
diagnostics: Run conductivity baseline profile only (no column) to verify gradient accuracy
Prime both pump channels individually and check volumetric flow accuracy by gravimetric measurement
Check buffer A and B inlet filter cartridges — replace if > 3 months old
Verify delay volume setting in PurityChrom accounts for mixer volume + column inlet tubing
corrective_actions: Prime both AZURA Bio pump channels with 5 mL of respective buffer before gradient run
Replace buffer inlet filter cartridges (KNAUER biocompatible filters) if blocked
Run pump flow rate calibration in PurityChrom diagnostics panel
Add 0.5–1 min hold at each gradient step to allow accurate mixing
Correct delay volume in PurityChrom method (system delay volume typically 1–3 mL for AZURA Bio)
escalation_conditions: Gradient deviation > 5% after priming — pump seal or check valve failure; schedule KNAUER service

model: AZURA Lab Prep System / AZURA P 6.1L
symptom: Prep system pressure exceeds 200 bar (Lab Prep limit) or 400 bar (P 6.1L limit) during purification run
likely_causes: prep column fritted disc blocked by sample particulates or silica fines
mobile phase precipitation at preparative concentrations
incorrect pump head installed for the target flow rate
excessive injection volume causing sample overloading and column blocking
guard column not installed or frit exhausted
diagnostics: Remove column and measure system dead-volume pressure at same flow rate in PurityChrom
Check prep column back-pressure vs initial certificate from column vendor
Check pump head volume vs method flow rate: AZURA P 6.1L 50 mL head optimal range 5–40 mL/min
Reduce sample load by 50% and retry — if pressure drops, overloading was the cause
corrective_actions: Install or replace guard column (prep guard with matching chemistry and 4–10 mm ID)
Reduce sample concentration and increase injection volume to maintain same mass load at lower concentration
Filter sample through 0.45 µm Millipore filter before injection
Flush prep column at 5 mL/min with 100% organic solvent for 30 min to dissolve precipitated sample
Replace pump head with correct size for target flow rate range
escalation_conditions: Column pressure > 150% of initial after washing — column frit damaged; replace prep column

symptom: Target compound and close-eluting impurities not resolved in preparative run; fraction purity insufficient
likely_causes: sample overload exceeding column dynamic binding capacity
gradient not optimised for prep scale (analytical-to-prep scale transfer requires gradient adjustment)
column particle size or length not appropriate for target resolution
injection solvent too strong causing initial peak broadening
fraction collection timing offset from actual peak apex
diagnostics: Run the same method analytically to verify baseline resolution exists at analytical scale
Reduce injection mass by 10-fold and check if resolution improves — confirms overload
Check fraction collector timing offset: verify UV detector-to-collector delay volume in PurityChrom
Compare gradient start/end concentrations with analytical method
corrective_actions: Reduce mass load per injection by 50%; increase number of injections instead
Recalculate gradient delay volume for preparative system (prep systems have > 5 mL system volume vs < 1 mL analytical)
Calibrate fraction collector delay volume in PurityChrom using a visible dye standard
Optimise gradient steepness: flatten gradient over critical resolution pair by 30–50%
If peak tailing: increase injection solvent aqueous content (use < 50% organic in sample diluent)
escalation_conditions: Resolution Rs < 1.0 at 50% mass load — method re-development required at analytical scale first

symptom: UV detector saturated (reads full-scale or flat-top peaks) during high-mass load preparative run
likely_causes: high UV-absorbing analyte at excessive concentration passing through the UV flow cell
incompatible flow cell pathlength — prep UV cells typically 0.5 mm to prevent overload
incorrect UV wavelength selected — monitoring at absorption maximum during high-load run
high background absorption from sample matrix or mobile phase modifier
diagnostics: Check UV absorbance reading during blank injection — any baseline > 2.0 AU indicates UV absorption issue
Compare peak height at analytical load vs prep load: saturation occurs when peak > 2.5 AU
Verify flow cell pathlength installed in AZURA UVD/DAD (prep: 0.5 mm; standard: 10 mm)
corrective_actions: Switch to 0.5 mm pathlength preparative flow cell to reduce detector overload
Monitor at a less-absorbing wavelength (e.g., 254 nm when 210 nm saturates)
Set UV detector range to extended scale (e.g., 3.0 AU range) in knauerOS/ClarityChrom
Dilute sample loading concentration by 50% and increase number of injections
Use post-column 1:100 splitter before UV detector for very high-load runs
escalation_conditions: Detector flat-top peaks cause fraction collection trigger failure — use conductivity or ELSD as fraction trigger instead

symptom: Pump flow rate oscillates ±5% or more during prep run; gradient composition deviates from PurityChrom program
likely_causes: air entrainment in large-volume pump head (50 mL head is sensitive to air)
check valve wear or fouling at preparative flow rates
solvent inlet filter partially blocked causing suction cavitation
pump head seal wear at flow rates > 30 mL/min
mobile phase viscosity too high for pump head specification
diagnostics: Listen for clicking or rattling during pump operation — indicates cavitation or check valve failure
Gravimetrically measure actual flow rate vs set flow rate at 10, 25, and 50 mL/min
Prime pump at low flow (2 mL/min) for 5 min and check if instability disappears — confirms air in pump head
Replace inlet solvent filter and re-test
corrective_actions: Prime 50 mL pump head with 50 mL of mobile phase at 5 mL/min before use — removes all air
Replace inlet filter cartridge (KNAUER prep inlet filter)
Replace check valves (inlet + outlet) for AZURA P 6.1L — clean with isopropanol first
Replace pump seals per KNAUER P 6.1L seal maintenance schedule (every 12 months or 2000 hours)
Ensure mobile phase viscosity is within pump head specification
escalation_conditions: Flow rate deviation > 10% at rated speed after seal replacement — pump head inspection required; contact KNAUER service

symptom: Collected fractions show unexpected impurity peaks on analytical HPLC despite clean baseline in prep run
likely_causes: fraction collector tubing contaminated from previous purification campaign
carryover in prep UV flow cell — previous compound not fully washed out
prep column bleed — stationary phase degradation releasing UV-absorbing fragments
fraction collection delay time miscalibrated causing wrong fractions collected
splitter ratio drift causing incorrect trigger signal
diagnostics: Run blank injection (100% mobile phase A) and collect fractions — analyse by analytical HPLC to confirm clean fractions
Run a standard compound and check fraction collector timing by correlating UV trigger with analytically confirmed fraction content
Inspect fraction collector tubing for residue or deposits
corrective_actions: Clean fraction collector tubing and collection nozzle with 10% methanol/0.1% TFA, then 100% methanol, then mobile phase A
Flush prep UV flow cell with 100% methanol for 15 min between campaigns
Recalibrate fraction collector delay volume in PurityChrom using a coloured dye
If column bleed suspected: run blank gradient and analyse by LCMS — replace column if confirmed
Replace prep column if column bleed is confirmed by LCMS analysis
escalation_conditions: Contamination persists after cleaning — column bleed or system contamination requiring full system flush and column replacement

symptom: Air bubbles visible in prep pump or tubing; erratic flow rate; UV baseline spikes during run
likely_causes: insufficient priming of large-volume pump head before use
solvent reservoir running empty mid-run
solvent inlet filter above liquid level (tubing too short for reservoir)
mobile phase not degassed — dissolved gas released at low pressure after pump
cracked or loose inlet fitting on pump head allowing air ingress
diagnostics: Visually inspect inlet tubing from solvent reservoir to pump — check for air gaps
Prime pump manually at 5 mL/min for 5 min and observe if bubbles clear
Check solvent reservoir level — inlet filter must be fully submerged at all times
Inspect inlet fitting for cracks or loose compression nut
corrective_actions: Prime both pump channels at 5–10 mL/min with fresh degassed mobile phase until all air is expelled
Refill solvent reservoirs — never allow < 20% volume during run
Extend or replace inlet tubing so filter is always fully submerged at reservoir bottom
Degas mobile phase by vacuum filtration or use KNAUER inline degasser
Tighten or replace cracked inlet fitting (KNAUER PEEK or titanium fittings for biocompatible applications)
escalation_conditions: Air bubbles persist after priming — check valve failure; replace pump check valves

symptom: Solvent recycling valve not diverting waste fractions correctly; non-target fractions sent to collection
likely_causes: incorrect delay volume calibration for recycling valve in PurityChrom
UV threshold for recycling trigger set too low — collecting baseline noise as product
recycling valve actuator failure (mechanical or electronic)
peak shape distortion causing wrong trigger timing
solvent recycling tubing blocked or kinked
diagnostics: Run a standard compound with UV monitoring and manually verify when recycling valve switches vs peak apex timing
Check PurityChrom recycling trigger settings: UV threshold, delay volume, valve switching time
Manually test recycling valve by triggering from PurityChrom control panel — listen for audible click
Check recycling tubing for kinks or blockages
corrective_actions: Recalibrate recycling valve delay volume using a dye standard: measure time from UV peak apex to valve switch in PurityChrom
Increase UV trigger threshold above baseline noise level (typically 10–20 mAU above baseline)
Replace recycling valve actuator if manual trigger fails
Unblock or replace recycling tubing — ensure minimum bend radius is maintained
Consider time-based fraction collection as alternative to UV-triggered recycling
escalation_conditions: Valve does not respond to PurityChrom trigger commands — electronic or actuator failure; contact KNAUER service

symptom: Loss of sensitivity or unstable signal on Agilent InfinityLab Pro iQ Plus
likely_causes: ESI/AJS spray chamber contamination
nebulizer needle blockage
ion transfer capillary contamination
dirty spray shield
diagnostics: Run autotune in MassHunter and compare tune report (m/z 112, 118, 322, 622, 922 for ESI-L tuning mix) to last passing report — signal intensity decrease > 50% confirms source contamination
Check spray chamber for salt deposits or discoloration — remove spray shield and inspect inner surface with flashlight; white crystalline deposits indicate non-volatile buffer accumulation
Inspect nebulizer needle tip under magnification for partial blockage or corrosion — a partially blocked nebulizer produces poor spray quality manifesting as noisy or weak signal
Review system health dashboard in OpenLab CDS — check source temperature stability, vacuum readings, and gas flow rates against expected values
Monitor background mass spectrum in scan mode: elevated chemical noise baseline (> 1e4 counts) across the mass range indicates general source contamination versus specific mass interference
Compare TIC baseline level between cleaned source and current state: baseline increase > 3× indicates contamination requiring cleaning
Check ion transfer capillary entrance for brown-black deposits — matrix accumulation on the capillary entrance is the primary signal loss mechanism on the Pro iQ Plus

Verify drying gas and sheath gas temperatures are reaching setpoints: use MassHunter diagnostics to check actual vs. set temperatures — underheating due to heater degradation reduces desolvation efficiency
corrective_actions: Clean ESI spray shield: remove and sonicate in 50:50 methanol:water for 15 min, then in 0.1% formic acid in methanol for 10 min — dry with nitrogen gas before reinstalling
Sonicate ion transfer capillary in 50:50 isopropanol:water for 15 minutes — if heavily contaminated, use 1% formic acid in methanol for stubborn protein or lipid deposits
Replace nebulizer needle if clogged or corroded — use Agilent OEM nebulizer needle; generic needles may have incorrect bore diameter affecting spray quality
Run Auto Acquire after cleaning to verify signal recovery — compare tune report intensities to pre-cleaning values; expect > 80% recovery for successful cleaning
If using AJS source: clean sheath gas nozzle by removing and wiping with lint-free cloth moistened with methanol; clean dry gas heater inlet screen to ensure unrestricted gas flow
Implement a preventive source cleaning schedule: every 500–1000 injections for high-matrix work (biological fluids), every 2000–3000 injections for clean synthetic samples
After source cleaning, run 5–10 blank injections before resuming sample analysis to flush out residual cleaning solvent and stabilize the baseline
escalation_conditions: Sensitivity not restored after full source cleaning — ion optics or detector may be contaminated; contact Agilent service for internal source maintenance
Autotune fails repeatedly after cleaning — quadrupole or RF generator issue requiring service engineer
SAFETY: AJS source operates at high temperature (up to 400 °C) — allow source to cool to room temperature before handling any components; wear heat-resistant gloves if source is warm

symptom: Low signal intensity or poor detection limits on Pro iQ Plus G6170A
likely_causes: Suboptimal fragmentor voltage
Wrong ion source mode for analyte (ESI vs AJS vs APCI)
Mobile phase contains non-volatile buffers or ion-pairing agents
Incorrect polarity setting
Dirty ion optics
diagnostics: Check fragmentor voltage in method parameters: optimal fragmentor varies by compound MW — small molecules (< 300 Da) typically 70–130 V, peptides (> 500 Da) typically 150–250 V; incorrect voltage reduces signal by 10–100×
Verify ion source mode matches analyte properties: AJS (Agilent Jet Stream) provides superior desolvation for maximum sensitivity vs. standard ESI — check that AJS is selected in MassHunter method

Review mobile phase composition for MS compatibility: phosphate buffers, TRIS, and borate are non-volatile and cause severe ion suppression and source fouling — only volatile additives (formic acid, ammonium formate, ammonium acetate) are MS-compatible
Run system suitability check with reference standard: inject 100 pg/µL reserpine or 1 ng/µL caffeine and compare S/N to historical values — S/N drop > 50% indicates hardware issue

Check ESI polarity against analyte ionization properties: basic compounds (amines) ionize in positive mode [M+H]+; acidic compounds (carboxylic acids) in negative mode [M-H]- — wrong polarity gives zero signal
Verify capillary voltage (Vcap): optimal range 3000–4000 V for standard ESI; too low reduces spray efficiency, too high causes corona discharge and noise

Check gas flow rates against Pro iQ Plus specifications: nebulizer 15–60 psi (start at 35 psi), drying gas 5–13 L/min at 150–350 °C, sheath gas (AJS) 3–12 L/min at 250–400 °C — suboptimal gas conditions directly reduce sensitivity
Evaluate LC flow rate compatibility: ESI optimal at 0.1–0.6 mL/min; flows > 1 mL/min require post-column flow splitter to avoid source overload and ion suppression
corrective_actions: Optimise fragmentor voltage using MassHunter Optimizer: run flow injection analysis of analyte at fragmentor values from 50 to 300 V in 10 V steps and select voltage giving maximum signal
Switch to AJS ion source for sub-30 fg sensitivity if not already in use — AJS provides orthogonal spray and super-heated nitrogen sheath gas for superior desolvation

Replace non-volatile buffers (phosphate, TRIS) with volatile alternatives: 10 mM ammonium formate pH 3.5 or 10 mM ammonium acetate pH 6.8 — verify chromatographic performance is maintained after buffer change
Clean ion transfer capillary and spray shield: sonicate in 50:50 MeOH:water for 15 min, then 0.1% formic acid in MeOH for 10 min — dry with filtered nitrogen before reinstalling

Verify and optimise gas pressures: nebulizer 35 psi (start), drying gas 10 L/min at 300 °C, sheath gas (AJS) 11 L/min at 350 °C — increase gas temperature in 25 °C increments if desolvation is insufficient
Install post-column flow splitter if LC flow rate > 0.5 mL/min: direct 50–200 µL/min to MS, remainder to waste or UV detector — use a calibrated tee with appropriate restrictor tubing
After optimisation, save method parameters and run a 5-point calibration to confirm linearity is maintained across the concentration range
escalation_conditions: Sensitivity below specification after cleaning and optimisation — schedule Agilent PM visit for internal source and ion optics cleaning

SAFETY: Never operate the ESI source with the spray chamber door open — high voltage (3–5 kV) at the nebulizer is lethal; always close and latch the spray chamber before switching to standby or operate mode

symptom: Pro iQ Plus G6170A not connecting or communication error in OpenLab CDS
likely_causes: LAN cable disconnected or faulty
IP address conflict on lab network
OpenLab CDS instrument configuration incorrect
Firmware needs update
diagnostics: Check LAN cable connection at rear of Pro iQ Plus instrument and at the network switch — verify link LED is active on both ends; a flashing LED indicates physical layer connectivity
Ping instrument IP address from workstation command prompt: 'ping <IP_address>' — if no response, check network configuration; if response but OpenLab fails, the issue is at the software/driver level
Verify instrument configuration in OpenLab CDS Control Panel — confirm the correct instrument type (Pro iQ Plus G6170A), IP address, and communication port are configured
Check instrument front panel for error indicators — LED color codes: green = ready, amber = standby/warning, red = fault; note any displayed error codes for Agilent support reference
Check Windows Event Viewer for USB or network errors at the time of communication failure — correlating system events with instrument disconnection helps identify root cause
Verify Windows Firewall is not blocking OpenLab CDS communication ports — temporarily disable firewall and test; if instrument connects, add firewall exception for OpenLab
Test with a direct LAN crossover cable between PC and instrument (bypassing the network switch) to isolate switch or network infrastructure problems

Check if other Agilent LC modules (pump, autosampler, detector) communicate normally — if only the Pro iQ Plus is offline, the issue is instrument-specific; if all modules are offline, it is a system or PC problem
corrective_actions: Power cycle the Pro iQ Plus: switch off → wait minimum 2 minutes for turbo pump to decelerate safely → switch on → wait for status LED to turn green before reconnecting in OpenLab CDS
Replace LAN cable with a known-good Cat5e or Cat6 cable — verify link LEDs illuminate at both ends after cable replacement
Assign static IP to avoid DHCP conflicts: configure via instrument front panel menu (Setup > Network > IP Address); document the IP address in the instrument logbook
Reinstall instrument driver in OpenLab CDS: remove the instrument from the configuration, restart OpenLab services, then re-add with correct parameters
Update firmware via Agilent OpenLab CDS instrument update utility — ensure firmware version compatibility with OpenLab CDS version per Agilent compatibility matrix
Disable Windows USB Selective Suspend and network adapter power management: Device Manager > Network Adapter > Properties > Power Management > uncheck 'Allow computer to turn off this device'

If using a managed network switch: verify the port VLAN assignment matches the instrument subnet; consult IT to ensure the instrument port is not subject to network security policies that block communication
escalation_conditions: Instrument does not appear after power cycle and cable replacement — possible mainboard failure; contact Agilent service
Turbo pump does not spin up after power cycle (no audible whine within 2 minutes) — vacuum system fault; do not attempt further troubleshooting; contact Agilent service immediately

symptom: Ion suppression observed on Pro iQ Plus affecting quantitation accuracy
likely_causes: Co-eluting matrix components
High buffer concentration in mobile phase
Late-eluting compounds from previous injection
Contaminated LC system introducing background ions
diagnostics: Perform post-column infusion experiment: continuously infuse 100 ng/mL analyte standard via T-piece into column eluent while injecting blank matrix — signal dips at specific retention times reveal suppression windows
Compare neat standard vs matrix-matched calibration curves: calculate matrix factor (MF) = peak area in matrix / peak area in neat — MF < 0.8 indicates > 20% ion suppression
Check for ghost peaks from previous injections by running 2–3 blanks after high-concentration samples — late-eluting matrix components from previous injections can suppress signal in subsequent runs
Evaluate LC gradient and column selectivity: try alternative column chemistry (C18 vs. phenyl-hexyl vs. biphenyl) to shift analyte away from matrix-dense elution region
Monitor internal standard (ISTD) response across the sample batch: ISTD area RSD > 15% indicates variable ion suppression that will compromise quantitation accuracy
Inject blank matrix at increasing volumes (1, 5, 10, 20 µL) to determine the relationship between matrix load and suppression magnitude — if linear, reducing injection volume is effective
Run LC-UV trace in parallel with MS: compare UV chromatogram to identify co-eluting UV-absorbing matrix peaks in the analyte retention window — these are candidate suppressor compounds
Test ESI+ vs ESI- mode: some matrix components suppress one polarity more than the other — polarity switching may avoid suppression for specific analytes
corrective_actions: Increase chromatographic separation to resolve analyte from matrix-dense region: add isocratic hold, shallow gradient, or longer column to improve resolution at the analyte retention time
Reduce buffer concentration to minimum effective level — ammonium formate > 10 mM and TFA > 0.05% cause measurable ion suppression; titrate down to find minimum concentration maintaining retention
Add wash steps between injections to eliminate carryover: program 100% organic wash for 2–3 min between each injection, followed by re-equilibration
Use AJS source which provides improved desolvation and reduced matrix effects — AJS heated nitrogen sheath gas at 350–400 °C improves droplet evaporation in high-matrix samples

Implement sample preparation cleanup: protein precipitation with acetonitrile (3:1 v/v), phospholipid removal SPE (Agilent Captiva EMR-Lipid), or solid-phase extraction (Agilent Bond Elut) before injection
Use stable isotope-labeled internal standard (SIL-IS) co-eluting with analyte — SIL-IS experiences identical suppression and corrects for matrix effect variability across samples
Reduce injection volume to 1–2 µL to minimize matrix load on the ESI source — compensate with higher sample concentration if sensitivity allows
escalation_conditions: Ion suppression persists above 50% despite method optimisation — consider alternative sample preparation or different ionisation mode (APCI for non-polar thermally stable compounds)
Matrix factor varies > 30% between individual patient/lot samples — method validation will fail FDA/EMA bioanalytical criteria; redesign sample preparation

symptom: Excessive baseline noise in MS signal on Pro iQ Plus
likely_causes: Contaminated mobile phase solvents
Air leak in LC system or spray chamber
Electrical noise from nearby equipment
Worn electron multiplier
diagnostics: Run blank gradient with fresh LC-MS grade solvents from newly opened bottles — compare baseline noise level (peak-to-peak in counts) to historical qualification data; noise increase > 3× indicates contamination or hardware issue

Check for air bubbles in LC flow path: inspect transparent tubing sections visually; monitor pump pressure for oscillations > 2% amplitude — air in the flow path causes periodic baseline spikes correlated with pump stroke frequency
Inspect spray chamber seal and nebulizer assembly: remove spray shield and check O-ring seal for damage or chemical attack — damaged seals allow ambient air ingress that increases chemical noise

Review autotune electron multiplier voltage (EMV) — compare current EMV to the value recorded at installation; EMV increase > 200 V above original indicates detector aging and increased amplified noise

Monitor background mass spectrum in scan mode: identify specific m/z values contributing to noise — plasticizer peaks at m/z 149, 279 (phthalates) indicate plastic contamination; m/z 391, 413 (PEG oligomers) indicate polymer contamination from tubing or filters
Check vacuum system: verify foreline pressure reading in MassHunter diagnostics — foreline > 5 Torr indicates roughing pump degradation or vacuum leak that increases baseline chemical noise
Test at different scan speeds and mass ranges: if noise scales with scan rate, it is electronic noise from the detector or ADC; if constant, it is chemical noise from contamination
Verify LC pump seal condition: leaking pump seals introduce air and cause periodic baseline modulation at the pump stroke frequency (typically 0.5–2 Hz)
corrective_actions: Replace solvents with fresh LC-MS grade reagents from newly opened bottles — use Agilent or equivalent certified LC-MS grade solvents; organic solvents degrade within weeks after opening

Degas mobile phases thoroughly: use online vacuum degasser (verify all channels active) or sparge with helium for 15 min — dissolved oxygen causes baseline noise through redox reactions in the ESI source
Tighten all LC fittings and check for leaks using tissue paper at each connection — even micro-leaks introduce air that causes periodic baseline spikes
Replace spray chamber seal (O-ring) if worn or chemically degraded — use Agilent OEM seal to ensure correct material compatibility with mobile phase additives

If EM voltage is > 200 V above original setting, schedule EM replacement — note this is a service engineer task on the Pro iQ Plus; continued operation at high EMV increases background noise proportionally
Flush entire LC system (pump, degasser, autosampler, column, detector) with 100% methanol for 30 min to remove accumulated contaminants — then equilibrate with fresh mobile phase
Install inline solvent filter (0.2 µm PTFE) between each solvent bottle and the degasser inlet to trap particulates and prevent contamination from bottle handling
escalation_conditions: Baseline noise does not improve after solvent replacement and system cleaning — possible EM failure or vacuum leak requiring Agilent service
SAFETY: If unusual odor (hot oil, electrical burn smell) is detected from the Pro iQ Plus, power off immediately and do not restart — contact Agilent service for vacuum pump or electronics inspection

symptom: Retention times shift systematically when transferring a gradient HPLC method between instruments; early-eluting peaks shift more than late-eluting peaks; gradient elution profile appears offset in time
likely_causes: Dwell volume (gradient delay volume) differs between the source and target instruments — dwell volume is the volume from the gradient mixer to the column inlet
Different pump and mixer architectures: low-pressure mixing systems (quaternary) have larger dwell volumes (1–5 mL) than high-pressure mixing systems (binary, 0.2–1.5 mL)
Additional system tubing, inline filters, or pressure transducers on the target instrument increase system volume
Different autosampler architecture: flow-through needle vs. fixed-loop contributes different amounts to effective dwell volume
Gradient proportioning valve position differs between instruments, creating different mixing chamber volumes
diagnostics: Measure dwell volume on both source and target instruments: inject 0.1% acetone (v/v) in water with a step gradient from 0% B to 100% B at 1 mL/min, no column — dwell volume equals the time (in mL) from gradient step to 50% of UV step response at 265 nm
Compare measured dwell volumes between instruments — difference > 0.3 mL for HPLC (> 0.05 mL for UHPLC) will cause measurable retention time shifts for gradient-eluted analytes

Run the analytical method on both instruments with the same column and mobile phases: overlay chromatograms and measure retention time differences — early peaks shift proportionally more because they experience the full dwell volume delay
Calculate expected RT shift: ΔtR = ΔVdwell / flow rate — a 1 mL dwell volume difference at 1 mL/min causes a 1-minute shift in all gradient-eluted peaks

Check if selectivity (relative retention order) changes between instruments: pure dwell volume mismatch shifts all peaks by the same time offset; selectivity changes indicate additional factors (column, temperature, mobile phase)

Verify gradient proportioning accuracy on the target instrument: run dwell volume test at different compositions (10%, 50%, 90% B step) — non-linear step response indicates mixer or proportioning valve issue

Measure system suitability parameters (resolution, tailing, plate count) on both instruments using the same SST standard — parameters other than RT should be similar if dwell volume is the only difference
Document complete fluidic path from pump outlet to column inlet on both instruments: measure each tubing length and ID to calculate total pre-column volume
corrective_actions: Add an isocratic hold at the beginning of the gradient on the instrument with smaller dwell volume: hold time = (larger dwell volume − smaller dwell volume) / flow rate — this compensates for the dwell volume difference

Alternatively, on the instrument with larger dwell volume: reduce pre-column tubing length or use smaller-ID tubing to reduce dwell volume — use 0.12 mm ID tubing for standard HPLC, 0.075 mm ID for UHPLC

Install a mixing loop (variable-volume loop) on the low-dwell-volume instrument to increase its dwell volume to match the source instrument — available as aftermarket accessories from most HPLC vendors
Adjust the gradient time table on the target instrument: shift all gradient time points by ΔVdwell / flow rate to compensate — document this adjustment in the method transfer protocol
Re-validate the method on the target instrument with the adjusted gradient: run system suitability, accuracy, precision, and linearity as specified in the method validation protocol
For USP/EP compendial methods: adjust only the initial isocratic hold, not the gradient slope or composition — changing gradient slope may invalidate the compendial method compliance
Document the dwell volume of both instruments in the method transfer report: ICH Q2 and FDA guidance recommend recording instrument-specific parameters that affect method performance
escalation_conditions: Retention time differences cannot be explained by dwell volume alone (selectivity changes observed) — investigate column lot-to-lot variability, mobile phase pH, and temperature differences between instruments
Method transfer fails to meet system suitability criteria after dwell volume correction — complete method revalidation on the target instrument may be required per ICH Q2(R2)

symptom: Peak efficiency (plate count) significantly lower on the target instrument compared to the source instrument; peaks are broader and asymmetric despite using the same column and method conditions
likely_causes: Extra-column volume (band broadening) is larger on the target instrument — connecting tubing ID, length, detector flow cell volume, and fitting dead volumes all contribute
Incorrect tubing ID: standard HPLC tubing (0.17 mm ID) used where narrow-bore UHPLC tubing (0.075–0.12 mm ID) is required for sub-2-µm or narrow-bore columns
Fittings with dead volume at column inlet/outlet connections: worn ferrules, incorrect ferrule type, or gap between tubing end and column frit create mixing chambers that broaden peaks
Detector flow cell volume too large for the column peak volume: a 13 µL analytical flow cell broadens peaks from a 2.1 mm × 50 mm UHPLC column by > 30%
Autosampler injection volume or needle seat dead volume contributing extra band broadening
diagnostics: Measure extra-column band broadening on both instruments: replace column with zero-dead-volume union, inject uracil (1 µL, 0.1 mg/mL) at the method flow rate, and measure peak width at half-height — convert to volume (σ²_v) using flow rate
Compare extra-column variance (σ²_v) between source and target: acceptable extra-column variance is < 10% of total peak variance — for a 2.1 mm × 100 mm sub-2-µm column, target σ²_v < 3 µL²

Inspect all tubing IDs with a caliper or by flow resistance measurement: flow restriction at the analytical flow rate should match between instruments — higher restriction for the same flow rate indicates smaller ID (correct for UHPLC)
Check all fittings for dead volume: remove each fitting and inspect the ferrule impression — a gap between the ferrule seal point and the tubing end creates a dead volume pocket

Measure detector flow cell contribution independently: compare peak width with and without the detector flow cell in the path (use a tee to bypass) — large flow cells (> 5 µL) broaden narrow peaks significantly
Calculate theoretical peak volume for the first eluted peak: V_peak = 4σ = 4 × L × ε_t × A_c / √N — if observed peak volume is > 1.5× theoretical, extra-column broadening is significant
Test with a well-retained peak (k' > 5) and a weakly retained peak (k' < 2): extra-column broadening disproportionately affects early peaks because their intrinsic peak volume is smaller
Photograph or diagram the complete fluidic path from injector outlet to detector outlet on both instruments for side-by-side comparison
corrective_actions: Replace all post-injector tubing with minimum length and correct ID: 0.075–0.12 mm ID for UHPLC columns (< 2 µm particles, 2.1 mm ID), 0.12–0.17 mm ID for standard HPLC columns (3–5 µm particles, 4.6 mm ID)

Use zero-dead-volume fittings at column inlet and outlet: finger-tight fittings (e.g., IDEX MarvelX, Waters Viper) ensure tubing bottoms out against column frit with no gap — verify connection quality by checking for extra peaks or shoulders
Replace detector flow cell with appropriate volume: ≤ 500 nL for UHPLC, ≤ 2 µL for standard HPLC — use a 60 mm path length micro flow cell for equivalent sensitivity at reduced cell volume
Minimize autosampler contribution: use partial loop injection mode with small needle seat volume; flush needle seat between injections to prevent carryover contribution to band broadening
Cut tubing to minimum possible length between injector and column inlet (< 150 mm) and between column outlet and detector (< 200 mm) — every extra centimeter adds measurable extra-column volume
Re-measure extra-column variance after modifications and verify it meets the target (< 10% of column peak variance) — repeat system suitability test to confirm efficiency recovery
Document the final tubing configuration (lengths, IDs, fitting types) in the instrument qualification record — future instrument changes must maintain equivalent extra-column volume
escalation_conditions: Plate count on target instrument is < 60% of source instrument after all extra-column optimizations — column may be damaged from shipping or installation; test with a fresh column from the same batch
SAFETY: When modifying UHPLC tubing and fittings, always depressurize the system first — UHPLC systems operate at up to 1300 bar and loose fittings under pressure can cause high-velocity solvent jets

symptom: UHPLC gradient method transferred from one UHPLC platform to another shows retention time shifts of 0.1–0.5 min for gradient-eluted peaks; relative peak spacing may also change slightly
likely_causes: UHPLC systems have dramatically different gradient delay volumes depending on architecture: Waters ACQUITY (0.1–0.3 mL), Agilent 1290 Infinity II (0.07–0.5 mL depending on mixer), Shimadzu Nexera (0.08–0.2 mL), Thermo Vanquish (0.08–0.4 mL)
Different mixer volumes between instruments: 35 µL vs. 100 µL vs. 380 µL mixers are commonly available — larger mixers improve gradient composition accuracy but increase delay volume
Autosampler metering mode differences: flow-through-needle (Waters, Thermo) vs. split-loop (Agilent) contribute different amounts to effective system volume
System tubing and valve configurations differ between OEM installations and user-modified systems
Gradient proportioning accuracy differs: high-pressure binary mixing vs. low-pressure quaternary mixing can create subtle selectivity differences beyond simple delay
diagnostics: Measure gradient delay volume on both UHPLC systems using the acetone step gradient method: program 0→100% B step at 0.4 mL/min with no column, detect at 265 nm — delay volume = time to 50% step × flow rate
Compare delay volumes: UHPLC methods are extremely sensitive to delay volume differences — even 50 µL difference at 0.4 mL/min causes a 7.5-second RT shift

Run the complete method on both systems with the same column lot: overlay chromatograms normalized to the first eluting peak — constant time offset for all peaks confirms pure delay volume difference; variable offset indicates selectivity change

Measure mixer dispersion profile: instead of a step gradient, run a 1-minute linear ramp and compare the shape of the composition profile between instruments — differences indicate mixer volume and mixing quality differences

Test gradient accuracy at the target flow rate: program 10%, 30%, 50%, 70%, 90% B steps and measure actual composition at each step using UV absorbance of acetone — composition accuracy should be within ±0.5% for UHPLC
Compare peak widths between instruments: if peak widths differ > 15% for the same column and method, extra-column effects (not just delay volume) are contributing — see method-transfer-extra-column

Verify column temperature is identical on both systems: ±1 °C temperature difference causes ±0.5–2% RT shift for most reversed-phase analytes — use external calibrated thermometer to verify actual column temperature
Check if peak elution order changes: if selectivity reversal occurs, the issue extends beyond delay volume to fundamental mobile phase delivery differences (mixing linearity, proportioning accuracy)
corrective_actions: Adjust initial isocratic hold time to compensate for delay volume difference: on the system with smaller delay volume, add hold time = (VD_large − VD_small) / flow rate before the gradient starts
If available, use the same mixer volume on both systems: Waters ACQUITY systems allow mixer cartridge swaps (50 µL, 100 µL, 380 µL); Agilent 1290 II offers 35 µL, 100 µL, and 380 µL options
Use emulation modes if available: Agilent Method Suitability Diagnostic (MSD) mode, Waters Emulation Package, and Shimadzu i-DReC all simulate specific delay volumes from other platforms

For critical separations where selectivity changes with delay volume: adjust gradient starting composition by (ΔVD / gradient volume) × (B_final − B_initial) to compensate for composition offset at column head
Re-validate the transferred method on the target system: run full system suitability including resolution, tailing, plate count, and RT precision — all parameters must meet method specification
Document delay volume measurements and any method adjustments in the method transfer protocol — regulatory inspectors expect documented evidence of instrument equivalence

Consider converting gradient methods to use generic gradient programs normalized to column volumes (t/t0 or column volume equivalents) — this format is more transferable across systems with different delay volumes
escalation_conditions: Selectivity reversal or co-elution occurs after delay volume correction — method redevelopment on the target platform may be required; consult method development team
Resolution between critical pair drops below method specification (e.g., Rs < 1.5) after transfer — consider column or mobile phase adjustment specific to the target system

symptom: UV/DAD response factors differ between source and target LC-MS systems; quantitative results from UV channel do not agree between instruments despite identical injection volumes and sample concentrations
likely_causes: Different UV detector flow cell path lengths between instruments: standard analytical cells are 10 mm, semi-micro cells are 6 mm, and UHPLC/LC-MS cells are 3–5 mm — path length directly affects absorbance per Beer-Lambert law (A = εcl)
Flow cell volume mismatch causing different degrees of band broadening and dilution — larger cells dilute narrow peaks more, reducing apparent peak height while preserving area
Different detector types: diode array detector (DAD) vs. variable wavelength detector (VWD) may have different optical designs and stray light characteristics affecting linearity at high absorbance
Wavelength accuracy differences between detectors: 2 nm wavelength offset at an absorption maximum can cause 5–15% response difference depending on the spectral band shape
Reference wavelength settings differ between instruments causing different baseline compensation behavior
diagnostics: Verify flow cell path length on both instruments: check instrument configuration in software (OpenLab, Empower, Chromeleon) or physically inspect the flow cell specification label — expected path lengths: 10 mm (analytical HPLC), 6 mm (semi-micro), 3 mm (LC-MS with post-column split)

Inject the same concentration standard on both instruments and compare peak areas and peak heights: if area ratio matches path length ratio (e.g., 10 mm/6 mm = 1.67), path length difference is the sole cause
Run wavelength calibration on both detectors: DADs use holmium oxide or didymium internal standards — wavelength accuracy should be ±1 nm; compare calibration results between instruments
Compare UV spectra of a standard compound acquired on both detectors: overlay normalized spectra — differences indicate wavelength accuracy or bandwidth differences between detectors
Check detector linearity on both instruments: inject 5-point dilution series from LOQ to 150% of method concentration — compare Beer-Lambert linearity (R² > 0.999) between instruments

Verify reference wavelength settings: some methods use 360 nm reference for background correction at 254 nm — different reference wavelength settings cause different baseline subtraction and apparent response
Measure detector noise and drift on both instruments: run blank gradient and compare baseline characteristics — higher noise on one instrument reduces effective sensitivity
For LC-MS split systems: verify the actual split ratio by measuring flow rate to the UV detector and to the MS separately — split ratio variation directly affects UV response
corrective_actions: Normalize response factors by path length: multiply the response factor from the shorter-path instrument by (shorter path / longer path) to predict expected response on the longer-path instrument — use this correction factor in the quantitative method

Install matching flow cells on both instruments: if the source instrument uses a 10 mm cell, install the same 10 mm cell on the target — verify that back-pressure from the cell is compatible with the system

Recalibrate the method on the target instrument: run a fresh calibration curve with the same reference standards — this automatically accounts for all detector differences without requiring path length correction

Match wavelength settings exactly: set detection wavelength, bandwidth, and reference wavelength identically on both instruments — even 1 nm difference at a steep spectral slope causes significant response change
For LC-MS with post-column split: verify and document the split ratio on the target instrument; if different from source, adjust either the splitter or recalibrate to compensate

Use relative response factors (response relative to internal standard) rather than absolute response factors — internal standard correction compensates for path length and detector sensitivity differences automatically
Document all detector parameters (path length, cell volume, wavelength, bandwidth, reference wavelength, response time) in the method transfer protocol for regulatory compliance
escalation_conditions: Quantitative results differ by > 20% after path length correction and recalibration — investigate detector linearity, stray light, and optical degradation; schedule detector qualification per manufacturer protocol
Detector linearity fails (R² < 0.999 over method range) — detector lamp aging or optical contamination; replace lamp and clean flow cell before re-qualifying

issue_category: method transfer SST criteria not met
symptom: System suitability test (SST) fails on the target instrument after method transfer — resolution, tailing factor, plate count, RSD, or capacity factor fall outside acceptance criteria established on the source instrument
likely_causes: Cumulative effect of multiple instrument differences: dwell volume, extra-column volume, column temperature, detector response, and mobile phase preparation all contribute small deviations that compound
Column lot-to-lot variability: different column batch on the target instrument has slightly different selectivity, efficiency, or retention characteristics
Mobile phase preparation differences: manual vs. gravimetric preparation, pH meter calibration, buffer concentration accuracy all introduce method variability
SST criteria set too tightly on the source instrument — criteria based on a single instrument's performance may not be achievable across different hardware platforms
Environmental differences between laboratories: ambient temperature, humidity, and altitude (affecting mobile phase degassing) can affect chromatographic performance
diagnostics: Identify which SST parameter(s) fail: resolution < 2.0 (most common transfer failure), tailing > 2.0, plates < N_spec, RSD > 2.0%, or capacity factor outside range — each failure points to a different root cause
If resolution fails: measure individual peak widths and retention times — determine whether the failure is due to peak broadening (efficiency loss), selectivity change (retention time shift), or both

If tailing factor fails: compare peak shapes between instruments at the same injection mass — tailing that appears only on the target instrument suggests dead volume at connections or column inlet void

If plate count fails: run column test mix per manufacturer specifications and compare to column certificate — if column passes vendor specification but fails method SST, the SST criteria may be too stringent for the target system
If RSD fails: examine injection-to-injection variability — autosampler precision differences between instruments can cause RSD failures; run 10 replicate injections and calculate RSD

Compare system suitability results from the source instrument (last 3 months of data) to the target instrument: calculate the historical range and standard deviation — SST criteria should allow for inter-instrument variability
Run SST on the target instrument using a fresh column from the same manufacturer lot as the source instrument: this isolates column variability from instrument variability
Check mobile phase pH on both instruments using the same calibrated pH meter — 0.1 pH unit difference can shift selectivity sufficiently to cause resolution failure for closely eluting pairs
corrective_actions: Address the specific failing SST parameter: for resolution: adjust selectivity (pH, organic modifier, column temperature); for tailing: check fittings and dead volume; for plates: optimize extra-column volume; for RSD: verify autosampler precision

Adjust dwell volume compensation: add initial isocratic hold or modify tubing to match dwell volumes between instruments — this corrects the most common source of resolution failure in gradient method transfers

Use the same column lot on both instruments: request column manufacturer to reserve a single production lot for method transfer — lot-to-lot selectivity differences are common and can be the sole cause of SST failure

Prepare mobile phases identically: use the same balance, pH meter, and volumetric glassware; weigh buffer salts rather than measuring by volume — prepare a single batch and ship to both laboratories if feasible

Widen SST acceptance criteria based on inter-instrument variability data: ICH Q2(R2) and USP <621> allow adjustment of system suitability criteria during method transfer if justified by validation data
